## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{0}{0}{0}{0}{0}{100}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why does a capable model still need a precise contract around every call?_

Every capability an autonomous agent adds—from tool dispatch and long-term retrieval to sandboxed execution and self-correction—is assembled from discrete foundation model calls. If the interface contract governing a single invocation is ambiguous, every downstream subsystem inherits that fragility. A model proposal may appear syntactically sound and yet violate schema constraints, arrive past its execution deadline, or misrepresent external environment state. Treating the model as an infallible oracle obscures the primary systems reality: ungrounded token predictors produce candidate proposals across an untrusted boundary, not verified state transitions. Reliability cannot reside in the model weights; it must be enforced by the surrounding runtime through strict token budgets, deterministic schema validation, and independent verification. Within the H·S·A exposure space, the single call marks the baseline origin: a single bounded turn, zero carried state, and zero autonomous authority.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Explain the separate responsibilities of the foundation model, inference service, and agent runtime
- Construct a token-bounded request containing task messages, advertised tools, and generation limits
- Calculate how temperature and nucleus truncation reshape the candidate distribution without establishing correctness
- Diagnose response outcomes using completion status, structural validity, permission checks, and task evidence
- Distinguish the guarantees of grammar-constrained decoding from learned formatting and correct task values
- Estimate call latency and repeated-input work under explicit serving and prefix-reuse assumptions
- Evaluate interface representations using accepted outcomes and resource use under matched task budgets

:::
## One Turn of the Repair Loop {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-introduction}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_origin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with all three axes gray and only the origin dot highlighted in purple."}

*A single call runs one turn, carries no state, and holds zero ambient authority.*
:::

The repair agent (\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}) needs to inspect the connection-pool implementation before proposing a change. A model invocation that emits `read_file("src/pool.py")` produces only an unexecuted text string. The generation itself carries no side effects, leaving the surrounding runtime to determine whether the path exists, verify that the operation is permitted, execute the filesystem read, and feed the resulting observation back into subsequent prompts. Interleaving model-generated actions with runtime observations forms the core interaction loop formalized by ReAct [@yao2023react]. In an agent architecture, that loop decomposes into discrete, isolated inference steps, where the stability of the entire system depends on how the runtime manages each individual turn.

Interactive chat interfaces rely on human operators to resolve operational ambiguity. A person working in a chat window immediately spots a response truncated mid-sentence, evaluates whether a proposed shell command is safe to run, and tolerates variable generation delays. An autonomous agent removes that human supervisor. The runtime receives the completion purely as structured data and must programmatically resolve questions that human judgment handled implicitly: whether the prompt fit within the model's context window, whether generation completed normally or hit a hard output token ceiling, whether a syntactically valid tool request targets a resource within permitted workspace bounds, and how much latency and financial budget the invocation consumed. Unstructured reply text cannot answer these operational questions. A runtime that attempts to deduce execution state by scraping raw output strings inevitably fails, whether by applying truncated code patches or executing commands outside its intended environment.

Eliminating these failure modes requires a formal call contract between the agent runtime and the model inference service. This contract governs both directions of the interface: the outbound request (specifying message history, advertised tool definitions, and token limits) and the inbound execution record (specifying payload structure, completion stop reasons, and token consumption). It also dictates the defensive validation pipeline the runtime applies before dispatching any proposed action, alongside accounting for the latency and input re-computation costs incurred by each invocation. Rather than assuming model reliability, the contract treats the inference service as an untrusted, probabilistic generator. By recording verified execution facts at each boundary, the contract ensures that the runtime—not the foundation model—retains deterministic control over control-flow decisions.

Tracing this lifecycle through the systems stack follows a single invocation from initial request dispatch to its ultimate resource cost. @Sec-vol3-foundation-model-role establishes the division of responsibility among the foundation model, the inference service, and the agent runtime, tracing the repair agent's inspection request through to its resulting environment observation. At the token boundary, @Sec-vol3-foundation-model-tokenization measures how prompt text maps into discrete context allocations, while @sec-vol3-foundation-model-autoregressive details how the inference engine decodes candidate tokens sequentially under varying sampling configurations. Because raw model outputs cannot be trusted implicitly, validating the returned candidate demands three complementary defense layers: structural checks verify syntactic soundness (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-continuations), service-level status records determine whether generation concluded cleanly or stalled against resource limits (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract), and grammar-constrained decoding enforces schema validity directly at the logits level during generation (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-grammar-constrained). Finally, sustainable agent systems require rigorous resource accounting: @Sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost models the latency and financial cost across multi-turn trajectories with prompt caching, and @sec-vol3-foundation-model-interface-design compares competing tool representations under a matched operational budget.
## The Model Invocation Boundary {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-role}

When an agent executes an operation—such as issuing `read_file("src/pool.py")`—the request traverses three distinct architectural components: the foundation model, the inference service, and the agent runtime. The foundation model[^fn-foundation-model-term] computes conditional probability distributions over token sequences given a prompt context. The **inference service**\index{Inference service!definition} hosts the model weights, executes forward passes on hardware accelerators, applies generation parameters, and packages the resulting tokens into a response envelope. The agent runtime orchestrates the broader task: it constructs the prompt, tracks resource budgets, validates generated candidates, and decides whether an action should actually execute against the host environment. Even when all three components reside on a single physical host, share an operating system process, or run within the same security domain, their interfaces maintain a crucial boundary: generated content remains strictly isolated from the decision to act on it.

[^fn-foundation-model-term]: **Foundation Model**: @bommasani2021opportunities coined the term for a model trained on broad data at scale and adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks, warning that such homogenization allows model defects to pass directly into every system built on top of it. For autonomous agents, the warning is concrete: every runtime that invokes the same model and serving path inherits identical failure modes at once. For this reason, the runtime, rather than the model, must hold all operational checks. \index{Foundation model!term origin}

::: {#dfn-vol3-proposal .callout-definition title="Proposal"}

A ***proposal***\index{Proposal!definition} is model output that specifies a candidate action or answer for the runtime to evaluate, carrying zero ambient authority and producing no external side effects until the runtime explicitly validates, authorizes, and executes it.

1.  **Significance**: Every external effect of an agent depends on an explicit runtime decision. Because the model call possesses zero ambient authority, a rejected proposal costs one inference invocation rather than an unintended modification to the environment. That invocation still consumes resources and counts toward $C_{\text{attempt}}$ in the cost per accepted task (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task).
2.  **Distinction**: A proposal must not be confused with an *effect* (a state change executed by the runtime after authorization) or an *observation* (the runtime's factual record of what an operation returned). Emitting `read_file("src/pool.py")` is merely a proposal; the file contents subsequently retrieved from disk and supplied to the next call constitute an observation.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Logging a tool request as an executed action, or accepting a model's textual claim that "the file has been read" as an empirical observation, allows fluent prose to stand in for operational evidence.

:::

### Messages and tool definitions {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-messages-tool-definitions}

The runtime structures interaction with the model through an ordered sequence of role-tagged messages\index{Model invocation contract!messages and roles}. A `system` message establishes application instructions, operational constraints, and behavioral policies. A `user` message specifies the task objective or developer prompt, while an `assistant` message records earlier model generations. When the runtime executes an action, it supplies the resulting output as a `tool` message containing the raw observation. Tagging content with a role structures the prompt context for the model's attention mechanism, but the tag itself provides no security guarantees: role labels organize the token stream, while the runtime remains responsible for verifying whether the content is authentic and whether it adheres to the task contract.

Alongside the message history, the invocation payload advertises the tools available to the model and specifies their expected argument schemas. In @lst-vol3-model-request, the runtime declares a file-reading tool with a single required string parameter. The JSON-schema definition informs the model of the syntax required for valid proposals, but the schema defines only the interface; the runtime enforces workspace sandboxing and filesystem permissions independently.

::: {#lst-vol3-model-request lst-cap="**A bounded inspection request**: This provider-neutral record separates model-visible messages and tool definitions from the configuration and limits governing the call. Symbolic values stand for settings chosen by the runtime; the field names do not prescribe a vendor API."}
```yaml
model_config: repair-model/config-a
messages:
  - role: system
    content: Propose the next inspection for the assigned repair.
  - role: user
    content: Inspect the connection-pool locking logic in src/pool.py.
tools:
  - name: read_file
    arguments_schema:
      type: object
      properties: {path: {type: string}}
      required: [path]
      additionalProperties: false
limits:
  max_output_tokens: K_max
  deadline: T_max
sampling: selected_sampling_settings
```
:::

The `model_config` identifier explicitly binds the request to a specific model version, weights checkpoint, and serving profile. Sampling controls govern how the inference service selects output tokens from the model's predicted probability distribution. Concurrently, resource bounds protect the system from runaway execution: `max_output_tokens` ($K_{\text{max}}$) caps the decoding budget to prevent unbounded generation, while `deadline` ($T_{\text{max}}$) establishes a strict timeout against queue delays and serving stalls. Specifying these bounds in the request record is effective only when the inference service or the client runtime actively enforces them during generation.

When generation concludes, the inference service returns free-form text, a structured tool proposal, or a service error. A runtime adapter normalizes these provider-specific responses into a uniform envelope, as illustrated in @lst-vol3-model-response. In this example, the service reports a completed generation pass that produced a structured tool request: a proposal to inspect `src/pool.py`, representing a single step toward diagnosis before any repair is verified.

::: {#lst-vol3-model-response lst-cap="**A returned tool proposal**: Response kind identifies what the payload represents, while status and stop reason describe the invocation. Usage counts describe consumed generation resources, not progress on the repair."}
```yaml
kind: tool_request
payload:
  name: read_file
  arguments: {path: src/pool.py}
status: COMPLETED
stop_reason: tool_request
usage: {input_tokens: S, output_tokens: K}
```
:::

Here, `kind` indicates how the runtime parser must interpret the payload. The normalized `status` confirms that the transport and generation protocols completed under the adapter's contract, while `stop_reason` captures the **stop reason**\index{Stop reason!definition} reported by the serving engine. This signal reveals why decoding terminated: whether the model generated a designated tool-call sequence, emitted an end-of-sequence token, or halted because it reached the token ceiling. The `usage` block tallies resource consumption, tracking $S$ input tokens processed and $K$ output tokens emitted. Accurate accounting across invocations prevents context-window overflow and provides the raw telemetry needed to monitor operational costs; when an upstream provider omits token accounting, the runtime must record the usage as missing rather than silently recording zero consumption.

@Fig-vol3-model-call-surface illustrates the complete invocation lifecycle, tracing how request artifacts enter the model and how response payloads route through the agent runtime.

::: {#fig-vol3-model-call-surface fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Model Call Surface**: The request carries messages, tool definitions, and limits into a model with frozen weights, which returns a proposal with a stop reason and usage counts. Every arrow out of the response lands in the agent runtime. The runtime validates and authorizes a tool call before anything runs, returns the result as a new message for the next call, sends a finished answer to verification, and quarantines output cut off at its limit." fig-alt="Diagram with a request box listing messages, tools, and limits, an arrow to a model box that samples one token per step with frozen weights, and an arrow to a response box listing text, tool calls, stop reason, and usage. Below, an agent runtime box routes on stop reason: a tool call goes to validate and authorize, then run in sandbox, then back to the request as a tool message; end of turn goes to verify; output limit goes to quarantine."}
![](images/svg/model_call_surface.svg)
:::

### Proposals and observations {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-proposals-observations}

When the runtime receives a tool proposal, it must not execute the action blindly. Instead, it routes the payload through a strict sequence of validation and authorization stages. First, the runtime validates structural conformance, ensuring that the proposed arguments match the declared schema (for example, confirming that `path` is a string rather than an arbitrary shell command). Next, it checks the arguments against the task's authorization policy: advertising `read_file` grants the model permission to propose file reads, but confers no right to access arbitrary paths. The runtime must verify that `src/pool.py` resolves within the task's allowed workspace rather than escaping to sensitive host locations through directory traversal. Once authorized, tool execution proceeds entirely outside the model invocation, typically within an isolated sandbox or container with explicit execution timeouts.

After the tool executes, the runtime captures the empirical outcome and prepares the subsequent invocation context. It appends the model's prior `assistant` proposal and pairs it with a corresponding `tool` message containing the resulting observation—in this case, the bounded file excerpt. Where the API supports correlation identifiers, the observation explicitly references the call identifier of the proposal it answers, preventing ambiguity during parallel or multi-tool executions. Operational errors, such as a missing file or an access permission denial, must be captured faithfully as observations rather than swallowed or masked by synthesized content. Models rely on accurate negative feedback to revise their strategies and recover from errors. Furthermore, whenever the runtime truncates tool output to preserve token headroom, the observation must clearly demarcate the omission so that the model does not mistake an excerpt for the entire file.

The model in the subsequent invocation observes the tool output solely because the runtime reconstructs and supplies the updated context window. Foundation models are stateless token predictors: they retain no internal memory of previous requests or intermediate executions. While session identifiers or server-side prefix caching can optimize latency by reusing key-value cache states across turns, the runtime remains the sole authority governing which messages enter the prompt. This separation also exposes temporal subtleties. A stored file excerpt reflects only the state of the workspace at the moment of inspection; if a subsequent command modifies the file on disk, the in-context observation becomes stale. The prompt records historical evidence rather than an active binding to the filesystem.

This operational reality exemplifies the fail-plausible dynamics analyzed in @sec-vol3-intro-fail-plausible. A model can emit a syntactically pristine proposal targeting the wrong source module, or generate a compelling analysis grounded in an obsolete observation. Emitted tokens often appear convincing even when the underlying reasoning or environment state is completely disconnected from reality. Robust agent engineering therefore requires treating status, schema structure, security authorization, and empirical evidence as distinct, non-fungible properties of the interaction.

The operational responsibilities summarized in @tbl-vol3-foundation-model-responsibilities emerge directly from these architectural distinctions. These requirements apply universally, whether the model executes within the local process or behind a remote network API.

| Model term                  | Runtime responsibility                                                       | Failure if the runtime ignores it                                     |
|:----------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Context window**          | Count the complete input representation and reserve output headroom          | Rejected request or insufficient room for a complete response         |
| **Sampling settings**       | Choose supported settings and retain them with the request and output        | Unexplained variation or an unjustified assumption of reproducibility |
| **Tool call**               | Check the proposal, authorize access, and return the actual tool observation | A proposed operation mistaken for an executed or permitted one        |
| **Stop reason**             | Interpret it with normalized status before treating the payload as complete  | An interrupted or refused response treated as a finished candidate    |
| **Fluent but wrong output** | Evaluate the relevant claim using checks and observations with stated limits | Credibility mistaken for evidence of the intended property            |
| **Successful response**     | Distinguish delivery and generation completion from task acceptance          | A completed call recorded as a successful repair                      |
: **What the runtime owns around a model call**: Each feature of the call creates an obligation outside the model's generated content. Satisfying one obligation does not discharge the others. {#tbl-vol3-foundation-model-responsibilities}

The request and response records define the operational boundary governing model invocations. Messages supply context, tool definitions define candidate proposals, and the runtime mediates all transitions to external state. Before an inference engine can admit a request, however, the entire payload must fit within the model's context window and generation limits. Enforcing those constraints requires measuring the request in tokens rather than relying on coarse approximations such as character counts, messages, or source files.
## Discrete Token Representation {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-tokenization}

When an automated repair agent appends a connection-pool source file and a compiler diagnostic to its message history, the payload expands rapidly. Naive metrics like file counts or raw character counts cannot determine whether the next request will fit within the model's capacity. Under the hood, role delimiters, tool schemas, system prompts, file paths, and source code all serialize into a single sequence of discrete units before entering the neural network. The true operational budget is the token count of that fully assembled sequence, measured strictly against the model's specific tokenizer and wire format.

### Tokens in the serialized request {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-serialized-request-tokens}

A **tokenizer**\index{Tokenizer!definition}\index{Tokenization|see{Tokenizer}} maps text into identifiers from a finite vocabulary. Subword methods represent frequent fragments compactly while breaking unfamiliar words and identifiers into smaller pieces [@sennrich2016subword]. **Byte-pair encoding**\index{Byte-pair encoding!definition}[^fn-bpe-compression-origin] learns repeated combinations of smaller units; other tokenizers use different segmentation rules, and some learn them directly from raw text without assuming word boundaries [@kudo2018sentencepiece]. A token may represent a word, part of a word, whitespace, punctuation, or a combination of these. Token boundaries therefore need not coincide with the boundaries of a source-code identifier or a JSON field.

[^fn-bpe-compression-origin]: **Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)**: The algorithm began as a data-compression scheme that repeatedly replaces the most frequent pair of adjacent bytes with an unused symbol [@gage1994bpe]; @sennrich2016subword repurposed the same merge rule to build open vocabularies for neural translation. Because the merges are learned from the training corpus's frequencies, the token cost of a string reflects how common it was in that corpus, so an unusual identifier or path can split into more tokens than a common word of the same length, and the runtime must count rather than estimate. \index{Byte-pair encoding!compression origin}

Indentation alone alters the resulting sequence. Under the standard `cl100k_base` byte-pair vocabulary, for example, the unindented line `def get_user_id():` encodes as five tokens beginning with `def` (identifier 755). Indenting that exact line by four spaces yields six tokens: three leading spaces (262), followed by ` def` with the fourth space fused to the keyword (711), and finally the remaining four tokens. Whereas a traditional compiler lexer identifies the same keyword token across both indentation levels, the model receives entirely different numerical identifiers. @Fig-vol3-token-ast-mismatch contrasts these two tokenizations against a compiler lexer's structural view.

::: {#fig-vol3-token-ast-mismatch fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**One Keyword, Two Token Sequences**: The same Python line passes through a compiler lexer (top) and a byte-pair tokenizer (bottom). The lexer records indentation as block structure and emits the same keyword and identifier for both lines. The tokenizer absorbs the fourth space into the keyword, so the indented line opens with two tokens that do not appear in the unindented one; only the four tokens after the keyword are shared. Identifiers are from the `cl100k_base` vocabulary." fig-alt="Two stacked panels. Top panel, compiler lexer: the lines def get_user_id(): and the same line indented by four spaces each map to the tokens def keyword, get_user_id identifier, open parenthesis, close parenthesis, and colon; the indented line adds a dashed indent token labeled block depth. Bottom panel, byte-pair tokenizer cl100k_base: the unindented line maps to def 755, space get 636, _user 3398, _id 851, and parentheses colon 4658, labeled 5 tokens; the indented line maps to three spaces 262, space def 711, and the same four tokens, labeled 6 tokens. Tokens 755, 262, and 711 are highlighted in red, with a note that the fourth space joins the keyword and 711 replaces 755, and a bracket marks the four shared tokens."}
![](images/svg/token_ast_mismatch.svg)
:::

In an inspection request, the string `src/pool.py` functions as a clean path argument at the tool interface, yet it decomposes into a sequence of subword tokens at the model interface. Altering a file path, introducing indentation, or escaping source code inside a JSON payload shifts token boundaries unpredictably. Because these splits depend entirely on the active vocabulary and serialization scheme, neither JSON formatting nor punctuation imposes a constant token overhead relative to raw prose. Systems runtimes cannot infer prompt length from average character-to-token ratios; they must measure the exact byte sequence scheduled for transmission.

Structural framing introduces further overhead. Model APIs wrap messages in specialized control sequences that delineate roles, conversation turns, and tool definitions according to model-specific wire protocols. Counting only the application's payload strings—such as user instructions or tool outputs—ignores this structural envelope. If the application handles serialization locally, it must tokenize the fully formatted wire payload using the model's precise tokenizer. Conversely, when a managed remote service injects proprietary chat templates or handles hidden system wrappers, the application must rely on the provider's token-counting endpoint and documented admission policies. Because token vocabularies and merging rules differ fundamentally across model families, token counts from one model cannot serve as proxies for another.

This accounting discipline applies equally to output generation. A concise tool invocation consumes fewer output tokens than an elaborate textual explanation that embeds the same invocation, but the exact cost depends on how the tool call is serialized. Compact schemas reduce latency and token spend only if they retain the structural detail the runtime demands; stripping essential parameters, file paths, or error enumerations to shave tokens undermines the robustness of downstream execution.

### Output headroom {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-output-headroom}

Let $S$ denote the length of the fully serialized input prompt, $S_{\max}$ the total **context window**\index{Context window!definition} (the maximum sequence capacity spanning input and output tokens within a single invocation), and $K_{\max}$ the reserved generation allowance, or **output headroom**\index{Output headroom!definition}\index{Context window!output headroom}. In an architecture where input tokens and generated tokens share a unified context budget, an admission controller must enforce:

$$S \le S_{\max} - K_{\max}$$

This inequality guarantees that an incoming prompt cannot saturate the context buffer and starve the model of capacity to produce an answer. Real-world services often impose independent ceilings on input and output lengths alongside this shared context limit, requiring the runtime to satisfy both individual caps and the combined constraint. Furthermore, when modern reasoning models produce hidden chain-of-thought tokens, those latent tokens debit the generation budget just like user-facing text. A concise three-line visible response can easily exhaust a large generation reservation if the model generated hundreds of hidden reasoning tokens beforehand.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-invocation-token-budget
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ADMISSION HEADROOM FOR AN INSPECTION REQUEST (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-foundation-model-tokenization, token and image budgets.
# │ Goal: Separate input admission from reserved generation capacity.
# │ Show: Remaining input room and the effect of a model-specific image charge.
# │ How: Use hypothetical service counts; subtract reserved output and input
# │      from the combined window, then add the image contribution.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

class InvocationTokenBudget:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    window = 8_192  # hypothetical combined context limit, tokens
    output = 1_024  # scenario: reserved generation allowance, tokens
    text_input = 6_000  # scenario: complete serialized text request, tokens
    image_input = 2_048  # scenario: service-reported additional image charge

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    input_ceiling = window - output
    headroom = input_ceiling - text_input
    multimodal_total = text_input + image_input + output
    excess = multimodal_total - window

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(input_ceiling == 7_168, "Unexpected input ceiling")
    check(headroom == 1_168, "Unexpected remaining input headroom")
    check(multimodal_total == 9_072, "Unexpected multimodal total")
    check(excess == 880, "The image must exceed the reserved request budget")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    window_str = fmt_int(window)
    output_str = fmt_int(output)
    text_input_str = fmt_int(text_input)
    image_input_str = fmt_int(image_input)
    input_ceiling_math = fmt_math(rf"S_{{\max}} - K_{{\max}} = {window:,} - {output:,} = {input_ceiling:,}")
    headroom_math = fmt_math(rf"{input_ceiling:,} - {text_input:,} = {headroom:,}")
    multimodal_math = fmt_math(rf"{text_input:,} + {image_input:,} + {output:,} = {multimodal_total:,}")
    excess_str = fmt_int(excess)
```

Suppose the repair interface has a combined window of `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.window_str` tokens, and the runtime reserves `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.output_str` tokens for generation. Its input ceiling is `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.input_ceiling_math` tokens. If the fully serialized request occupies `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.text_input_str` tokens, we have `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.headroom_math` tokens of room for additional input while preserving the response allowance. The limits are scenario values, not a named model's specification.

If an incoming tool observation exceeds this remaining headroom, the admission check fails. At this juncture, the runtime faces an explicit engineering trade-off: it can compress prompt history, extract a narrower file slice, or route the call to an execution profile with a larger context window. Artificially shrinking the output allowance $K_{\max}$ to force admission is risky, as it leaves the model insufficient room to complete complex tool invocations or structured plans. Similarly, silently truncating tool outputs to squeeze them into the remaining margin can strip away the critical stack trace or diagnostic error that the agent needs to resolve the bug.

Even when a request satisfies admission checks, generation can still hit the output token ceiling mid-stream. In systems terms, the runtime must never confuse a syntactically well-formed prefix with a successfully terminated generation. A truncated JSON object may happen to pass a lenient parser if closed artificially, yet it remains an incomplete execution plan. While a partial payload provides valuable diagnostic telemetry, executing it as an intact tool call can cause downstream corruption. The formal invocation contract in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract formalizes this boundary through explicit status-first handling rules.

### Multimodal input accounting {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-multimodal-accounting}

When the repair task incorporates visual inputs—such as a screenshot of a failing diagnostic dashboard or UI render—context accounting shifts from character tokenization to multimodal embedding. The model's vision front-end maps the visual input into a set of context positions. While vision transformers typically partition images into uniform patches [@dosovitskiy2021image], upstream preprocessing steps like dynamic tiling, resolution downsampling, and spatial pooling mean that the final count of reserved context tokens rarely matches raw patch counts.

Consider the earlier budget when adding this visual artifact. If the service reports that the image and its framing tokens require an additional `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.image_input_str` context positions, the total request demand expands to `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.multimodal_math` tokens. This total exceeds the `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.window_str`-token context window by `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.excess_str` tokens, triggering an immediate admission failure before dispatch. The orchestrator must intervene before calling the model. While downscaling the image can reduce its token footprint under some vision backends, aggressive compression risks obliterating fine-grained diagnostic clues, such as single-character error codes or minute trace graphs. Multimodal token budgeting is thus an optimization over information preservation, balancing fidelity against strict context bounds.

::: {#chk-02-context-exhaustion-quarantine .callout-checkpoint title="Admitting the next repair request"}

The repair agent is about to add a source excerpt and a diagnostic image to its next call. Its output allowance must remain available for a complete proposal.

- [ ] **Input budget**: Can you identify which message and tool-definition framing must be counted beyond the visible source excerpt?
- [ ] **Output headroom**: With the window fixed at `{python} InvocationTokenBudget.window_str` tokens and the image added, would halving the output reservation make the request fit? Compute the remaining excess, and state what the smaller reservation risks.
- [ ] **Generation status**: If a returned fragment parses successfully after the output limit is reached, can you explain why it is still not a completed candidate?

:::

Token accounting provides an indispensable gatekeeping mechanism: it establishes an upfront admission test for the complete request while reserving adequate operational headroom for the response. But context admission addresses only initial capacity. Once the model begins decoding, token-by-token autoregressive generation dictates how quickly that reserved headroom is consumed and whether the interaction terminates cleanly or truncates prematurely.
## Autoregressive Generation {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-autoregressive}

A client request specifies the conversation history and the catalog of available tool schemas, but the generated response remains open-ended and stochastic. In a software repair task, for example, the model might propose `read_file` on a specific configuration path, select an entirely different source directory, or emit an unstructured natural-language explanation instead. Systems engineers must understand how the engine generates this text to configure appropriate token budgets and sampling parameters. That understanding also clarifies why re-executing an API request against a live model produces a fresh distribution of behaviors, whereas replaying a recorded trace provides exact downstream determinism.

### Conditional token selection {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-conditional-token-selection}

Autoregressive language models generate text by decomposing the joint probability of a sequence into a product of conditional next-token distributions, a foundational framing introduced in early neural language modeling [@bengio2003neural]. Let $x_{1:S}$ denote the input tokens and $y_{1:K}$ an output sequence. Its conditional probability factors as

$$\Pr(y_{1:K} \mid x_{1:S}) = \prod_{t=1}^{K} \Pr(y_t \mid x_{1:S}, y_{1:t-1})$$ {#eq-autoregressive-factorization}

At output position $t$, the model with parameters $\theta$ produces one score, or **logit**\index{Logits!definition}, for each token in vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$:

$$\mathbf{z}_t = \mathbf{f}_\theta(x_{1:S}, y_{<t}) \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}$$

A decoding rule selects a token from these scores, and the chosen token is appended to the prefix for position $t+1$. Because every subsequent step conditions on all preceding tokens, early decisions cascade through the remainder of the trajectory. When a model emits a specific file path inside a `read_file` argument, for example, that string immediately conditions the emission of the closing syntax and subsequent reasoning tokens. The model generates this path purely from learned statistical associations without consulting the operating system to establish whether the file actually exists.

In an inference serving engine, the decode loop processes the prompt, computes next-token logits, selects an output token, appends it to the prefix context, and repeats this cycle until triggering a termination condition. Generation can terminate normally when the model emits an explicit end-of-sequence token or matches a caller-configured stop sequence. Alternatively, an execution engine may halt generation prematurely when reaching an output token limit, or abort unexpectedly due to an infrastructure timeout or network disconnect. Serving interfaces must report these stop reasons explicitly: receiving an incomplete JSON object due to a hit token limit requires different recovery handling than receiving a cleanly terminated tool call. Crucially, a clean stop sequence merely signals that the model finished generating text; it provides no guarantee that the underlying task succeeded.

Production Transformer implementations [@vaswani2017] eliminate redundant computation across decoding steps by maintaining a *key-value (KV) cache*:[^fn-kv-cache-derived] memory buffers that store intermediate attention keys and values derived from previously processed tokens. Reusing this state avoids recomputing projections for historical tokens at every step. For a fixed full-attention architecture and storage precision, retaining more tokens requires more cache capacity. This cache represents transient intermediate computational state rather than an authoritative audit log proving which tools executed or what their external effects were. Cache organization and capacity planning are developed in @sec-vol3-kv-cache; the direct operational consequence is that the prompt and generated output both contribute to a call's memory footprint and resource demand.

[^fn-kv-cache-derived]: **Key-Value (KV) Cache**: In causal attention, key and value vectors at a given position depend solely on that token and its predecessors, so once computed they remain static throughout subsequent sequence expansion. Retaining them in device memory turns each new decode step from full-sequence recomputation into a single new row projection per layer alongside a read of stored rows. Consequently, cache capacity and memory bandwidth, rather than floating-point arithmetic, become the primary operational constraints as context windows expand. \index{KV cache!why reuse is exact}

Because each generated token extends a dependent sequence, output length is the primary cost variable of a call, and the serving implementation sets its realized latency. Although the conditional dependence in @eq-autoregressive-factorization fixes the mathematical order of token choices, it does not mandate that hardware evaluate each token in an isolated forward pass. Techniques such as speculative decoding,[^fn-speculative-decoding-equivalence] for example, draft candidate token blocks with a small auxiliary model and score them in parallel with the target model, provably preserving the target output distribution [@leviathan2023fast; @chen2023accelerating].

[^fn-speculative-decoding-equivalence]: **Speculative Decoding**: A small draft model proposes several candidate tokens, and the target model scores them all concurrently in a single forward pass; a modified rejection-sampling rule accepts each drafted token with a probability that guarantees the accepted sequence matches the exact distribution of the target model sampling independently [@leviathan2023fast; @chen2023accelerating]. This guarantee is distributional rather than bitwise: it reduces the number of accelerator passes per generated token without altering the underlying candidate space, maintaining the same reproducibility characteristics discussed later in this section. \index{Speculative decoding!distribution preservation}

### Sampling controls {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-sampling-controls}

For positive **temperature**\index{Temperature (sampling)!definition}[^fn-sampling-temperature-origin] $\tau_{\text{temp}}$, softmax converts the logits into next-token probabilities:

$$\Pr(y_t = v \mid x_{1:S}, y_{<t}) = \frac{\exp\left(z_{t, v} / \tau_{\text{temp}}\right)}{\sum_{w \in \mathcal{V}} \exp\left(z_{t, w} / \tau_{\text{temp}}\right)}$$ {#eq-temperature-softmax}

Unit temperature ($\tau_{\text{temp}} = 1.0$) leaves the logits unscaled. Lowering a positive temperature amplifies logit disparities, sharply concentrating probability mass on higher-scoring tokens; raising it compresses logit differences and makes the distribution flatter. With a finite vocabulary and finite logits, the distribution approaches uniformity as temperature grows without bound. Systems engineers should treat temperature strictly as an entropy modulator rather than a confidence metric. Because next-token cross-entropy training minimizes sequence prediction error rather than calibrating scores as estimates of task success, high token likelihood does not verify that a completed response is logically sound or correct.

[^fn-sampling-temperature-origin]: **Temperature**: The nomenclature comes from statistical mechanics, where the Boltzmann distribution weights a state of energy $E$ by $\exp(-E/k_B T)$; reading each negative logit as an energy makes @eq-temperature-softmax mathematically identical. In thermodynamic systems, high temperature distributes particles across many states, whereas low temperature collapses the system toward its ground state. In language model decoding, scaling temperature balances candidate exploration against exploitation of the mode without altering which token scores highest. \index{Temperature (sampling)!Boltzmann origin}

**Greedy decoding**\index{Greedy decoding!definition} instead selects the maximum-scoring token: $\operatorname{argmax}_{v \in \mathcal{V}} z_{t,v}$, combined with a consistent tie-breaking rule. Given fixed logits and a fixed tie rule, that selection is deterministic. While serving APIs frequently expose greedy decoding through a temperature-zero setting, the runtime executes this via direct argmax selection rather than evaluating @eq-temperature-softmax with division by zero. As positive temperature approaches zero, softmax concentrates all probability mass on the maximum; if several logits share the maximum, that mathematical limit alone does not select among them.

Sampling can also restrict which tokens remain eligible. **Top-$k$ sampling**\index{Top-k sampling!definition} [@fan2018hierarchical] retains the $k$ highest-scoring tokens, according to a defined tie rule, and renormalizes their probabilities. **Top-$p$ sampling**\index{Top-p sampling!definition}, also called nucleus sampling, sorts tokens by descending probability and retains the shortest leading sequence whose cumulative mass reaches threshold $p$ [@holtzman2020curious], subsequently renormalizing that active set. Top-$k$ fixes the candidate count regardless of context, retaining implausible tail tokens when the distribution is peaked and cutting viable candidates when the distribution is flat. Top-$p$ resolves this rigidity by allowing the candidate pool size to adapt dynamically to distribution entropy. When temperature scaling and truncation are combined, their evaluation order and the runtime's numerical conventions form an explicit part of the decoding configuration.

Crucially, neither filter identifies valid file paths, truthful statements, or safe operations. A rare token may be essential to a correct identifier or software patch, while a highly probable continuation may propose an incorrect file name. Truncation filters alter the distribution of candidates exposed to downstream execution, and evaluation against external task criteria determines whether that modification improves performance.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/nucleus_truncation_margin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Five probability bars for tokens v1 to v5 at unit temperature. v1 is labeled 78 percent and v2 17 percent, both in blue under a bracket labeled top-p 0.90. v3, v4, and v5 are in red with a zero above each and the label tail cut."}

*Nucleus truncation keeps two tokens here and zeroes the whole tail.*
:::

```{python}
#| label: lego-logit-scaling-truncation
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LOGIT SCALING AND TRUNCATION (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-02-logit-scaling-and-truncation-on
# │ Goal: Compare temperature and nucleus sampling for the same hypothetical logits.
# │ Show: Sharpening and truncation redistribute probability, not correctness.
# │ How: Normalize exponentials, select a cumulative-probability prefix, renormalize.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_math, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent

class LogitScalingTruncation:
    """Sampling transformations for a fixed hypothetical vocabulary."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    logits = [12.0, 10.5, 9.0, 6.0, 3.0]
    tau_base = 1.0
    tau_sharp = 0.5
    p_nucleus = 0.90

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    exp_tau1 = []
    for z in logits:
        exp_tau1.append(math.exp(z / tau_base))
    sum_exp_tau1 = sum(exp_tau1)
    probs_tau1 = []
    for e in exp_tau1:
        probs_tau1.append(e / sum_exp_tau1)
    exp_tau05 = []
    for z in logits:
        exp_tau05.append(math.exp(z / tau_sharp))
    sum_exp_tau05 = sum(exp_tau05)
    probs_tau05 = []
    for e in exp_tau05:
        probs_tau05.append(e / sum_exp_tau05)
    sum_nuc = probs_tau1[0] + probs_tau1[1]
    p_nuc_v1 = probs_tau1[0] / sum_nuc
    p_nuc_v2 = probs_tau1[1] / sum_nuc
    tail_base = 1 - probs_tau1[0]  # probability of drawing any non-top token
    tail_sharp = 1 - probs_tau05[0]
    tail_ratio = tail_base / tail_sharp

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(sum(probs_tau1) - 1.0) < 1e-12, "Baseline distribution must normalize")
    check(abs(sum(probs_tau05) - 1.0) < 1e-12, "Sharpened distribution must normalize")
    check(abs(probs_tau1[0] - 0.7840) < 0.001, "Unexpected tau=1.0 top prob")
    check(abs(probs_tau05[0] - 0.950324648968) < 1e-9, "Unexpected tau=0.5 top prob")
    check(abs(sum_nuc - 0.9589) < 0.001, "Unexpected nucleus denominator")
    check(probs_tau1[0] < p_nucleus <= sum_nuc, "Nucleus must contain exactly two tokens")
    check(abs(p_nuc_v1 - 0.8176) < 0.001, "Unexpected nucleus v1 prob")
    check(abs(p_nuc_v2 - 0.1824) < 0.001, "Unexpected nucleus v2 prob")
    check(abs(p_nuc_v1 + p_nuc_v2 - 1.0) < 1e-12, "Nucleus must normalize")
    check(3 < tail_ratio < 6, "Halving temperature should shrink the non-top tail several-fold")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    logits_math = fmt_math(rf"\mathbf{{z}}_t = [{', '.join(f'{v:g}' for v in logits)}]")
    base_vector_math = fmt_math(rf"\mathbf{{p}}_{{\tau_{{\text{{temp}}}}=1}} \approx [{', '.join(f'{v:.4f}' for v in probs_tau1)}]")
    sharp_first_str = fmt(probs_tau05[0], precision=4, commas=False)
    sum_exp_tau1_str = fmt(sum_exp_tau1, precision=1, commas=False)
    tau_base_str = fmt(tau_base, precision=0, commas=False)
    tau_sharp_str = fmt(tau_sharp, precision=1, commas=False)
    top_mass_pct_str = fmt_percent(probs_tau05[0], precision=1, style="prose")
    p_nucleus_str = fmt(p_nucleus, precision=2, commas=False)
    first_prob_str = fmt(probs_tau1[0], precision=4, commas=False)
    second_prob_str = fmt(probs_tau1[1], precision=4, commas=False)
    nucleus_mass_str = fmt(sum_nuc, precision=4, commas=False)
    nucleus_first_str = fmt(p_nuc_v1, precision=4, commas=False)
    nucleus_second_str = fmt(p_nuc_v2, precision=4, commas=False)
    tail_base_pct_str = fmt_percent(tail_base, precision=1, style="prose")
    tail_sharp_pct_str = fmt_percent(tail_sharp, precision=1, style="prose")
    tail_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(tail_ratio, precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-02-logit-scaling-and-truncation-on .callout-notebook title="Temperature and truncation on the same logits"}

**Problem**: A hypothetical vocabulary $\mathcal{V} = \{v_1, v_2, v_3, v_4, v_5\}$ has logits `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.logits_math`, held fixed so that differences arise strictly from the decoding configuration. How much probability mass concentrates onto the top token when halving the temperature, and which tokens survive nucleus truncation?

**Math**: At temperature $\tau_{\text{temp}} =$ `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.tau_base_str`, the exponentiated logits sum to `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.sum_exp_tau1_str`. Normalizing each exponential by this partition sum yields the baseline distribution:

`{python} LogitScalingTruncation.base_vector_math`.

Halving the temperature to $\tau_{\text{temp}} =$ `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.tau_sharp_str` doubles the exponent of each term. Following normalization, the probability of the mode $v_1$ surges to `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.sharp_first_str`, capturing `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.top_mass_pct_str` of the total distribution. All lower-ranked tokens retain positive probability under untruncated softmax.

Returning to unit temperature and applying nucleus truncation with $p =$ `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.p_nucleus_str` evaluates cumulative probability mass. The lead token $v_1$ provides `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.first_prob_str`, which falls short of the threshold. Incorporating $v_2$ (`{python} LogitScalingTruncation.second_prob_str`) brings cumulative coverage to `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.nucleus_mass_str`, which satisfies the threshold and defines the active nucleus as $\{v_1, v_2\}$. Renormalizing across this active set assigns probability `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.nucleus_first_str` to $v_1$ and `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.nucleus_second_str` to $v_2$, while strictly zeroing the remaining tail tokens $\{v_3, v_4, v_5\}$.

**Systems insight**: Temperature governs candidate diversity. Halving temperature compresses the non-top probability tail from `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.tail_base_pct_str` to `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.tail_sharp_pct_str`, achieving a `{python} LogitScalingTruncation.tail_ratio_mult_str` reduction, whereas nucleus truncation eliminates the tail entirely. Repeated calls produce diverse outputs only when probability mass occupies this tail—the exact stochastic resource harvested by the search and consensus strategies in @sec-vol3-test-time-compute. Because neither transformation ensures that the highest-scoring candidate is correct, engineering teams configure decoding parameters based on empirical task pass rates rather than raw model likelihood.

:::

### Repetition and replay {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-repetition-replay}

Greedy decoding removes sampling variance from a fixed logit vector, but it does not guarantee end-to-end reproducibility across served API calls. In distributed production infrastructure, identical input requests frequently encounter different serving nodes, hardware accelerator revisions, or software runtime configurations. Subtle variations in floating-point reduction order[^fn-float-reduction-order] can shift closely contested logits in their least significant bits; flipping an argmax selection at position $t=1$ permanently alters all downstream conditioning. Similarly, configuring a fixed pseudorandom seed constrains the sampling generator without eliminating numerical non-determinism across backend kernels or cluster deployments. True reproducibility requires a strictly pinned execution environment and software contract, extending well beyond setting $\tau_{\text{temp}} = 0$. Real-world production incidents illustrate how infrastructure changes in the serving fleet can dramatically alter generation behavior while caller requests remain identical.

[^fn-float-reduction-order]: **Floating-Point Reduction Order**: Floating-point addition lacks associativity because intermediate calculations undergo rounding at each operation [@goldberg1991]. Parallel attention and reduction kernels that accumulate dot products across differing thread block dimensions or dynamic batch sizes execute summation in varying orders, yielding minor discrepancies in the least significant bits of logit tensors. When two top candidates have nearly identical values, this numerical divergence suffices to invert a greedy selection, redirecting the subsequent autoregressive path. \index{Floating-point arithmetic!nondeterministic reduction}

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-fm-serving-postmortem
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SERVING-PATH INCIDENT FIGURES (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: ws-02-anthropic-serving-bugs-2025 and the replay fallacy in
# │          @sec-vol3-foundation-model-fallacies.
# │ Goal: Carry the incident's reported shares as named, sourced inputs.
# │ Show: Worst-hour share of one model's requests misrouted; share of one
# │       tool's users with at least one misrouted message.
# │ How: Values as reported in anthropic2025postmortem; no computation.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_percent

class ServingPostmortem:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    worst_hour_share = 0.16  # sourced: anthropic2025postmortem, worst hour, one model's requests misrouted
    user_share = 0.30  # sourced: anthropic2025postmortem, approx. share of coding-tool users affected

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Reported values only.

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 < worst_hour_share < user_share < 1, "Reported shares must be fractions in source order")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    worst_hour_pct_str = fmt_percent(worst_hour_share, precision=0, style="prose")
    user_pct_str = fmt_percent(user_share, precision=0, style="prose")
```

::: {#ws-02-anthropic-serving-bugs-2025 .callout-war-story title="Three serving bugs behind unchanged requests (2025)"}

**Context**: Between August and early September 2025, three separate infrastructure bugs intermittently degraded the responses of Anthropic's Claude models [@anthropic2025postmortem]. These defects stemmed entirely from the serving infrastructure rather than caller requests or model weights.

**Mechanism**: A front-end routing defect directed standard traffic to server clusters configured for extended context windows, while session stickiness trapped follow-up requests on those misconfigured nodes. Concurrently, an improperly deployed kernel optimization on a specialized accelerator cluster occasionally assigned outsized probability to improbable tokens. Finally, an optimization in the token-selection pipeline triggered a compiler bug: an approximate top-$k$ routine with mixed-precision subroutines emitted incorrect tokens under specific dynamic batch sizes.

**Impact**: During peak impact, the routing failure corrupted `{python} ServingPostmortem.worst_hour_pct_str` of requests to one production model, and approximately `{python} ServingPostmortem.user_pct_str` of active coding agent users encountered at least one misrouted interaction. Generated responses exhibited foreign-language script insertions within English prose and syntax anomalies in generated source code. Automated regression suites initially missed these failures because downstream models frequently masked isolated token corruptions, and intermittent runtime conditions meant an identical prompt could succeed on one invocation and fail catastrophically on the next.

**Fix**: Engineers rolled back the offending kernel deployments, corrected cluster routing rules, and replaced the approximate top-$k$ kernel with an exact selection routine running in 32-bit floating-point precision, trading a minor throughput penalty for numerical stability. Anthropic subsequently deployed continuous canary evaluations across production fleets to catch subtle generational drift.

**Systems lesson**: Output distributions reflect the concrete serving pipeline just as heavily as the model weights or input context. Corrupted tokens arrived packaged in well-formed HTTP payloads and cleanly closed generation blocks, illustrating the classic fail-plausible failure mode in machine learning systems. Robust agent architectures must log full call-level metadata—capturing runtime versions, routing tags, and sampling parameters—while subjecting every proposed action to external environment validation regardless of nominal generation success.

:::

Production failures of this nature define the baseline instrumentation required for agentic infrastructure. Comprehensive diagnostic logs must capture the exact prompt payload, model and tokenizer revision hashes, decoding hyperparameters, configured token limits, and any backend routing or seed metadata. Alongside input parameters, the system must record the raw response payload, the explicit finish reason, and token usage metrics. When diagnosing downstream agent failures, developers should distinguish between replaying a recorded trajectory and re-querying the model. Replaying a recorded trace isolates downstream execution logic from model nondeterminism, whereas issuing a repeated API call tests the resilience of the agent across sampling variations. Rigorous evaluation frameworks must measure and report this repeated-call variance rather than assuming consistent single-call execution.

Ultimately, an agent runtime ingests candidate tokens produced under a specific decoding configuration and terminated by a specific boundary condition. Even an uncorrupted, high-probability `read_file` proposal might reference an absent path or violate sandbox directory restrictions. The autoregressive generation process determines how a candidate sequence is synthesized; downstream systems must establish the verification harnesses and guardrails required to evaluate whether that sequence can safely execute.
## Candidate Sequence Verification {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-continuations}

Consider an automated repair agent that issues a tool call to `read_file` with `path` set to `src/pool.py`. The generated payload might conform strictly to the advertised schema, but syntactic conformance guarantees nothing about the underlying filesystem. The target file might not exist in the active workspace. Worse, a path pointing to private credential files outside the repository would parse with equal syntactic perfection. Generative inference produces a candidate token sequence; neither high statistical likelihood nor schema conformance determines whether the runtime environment can safely act on it.

The same distinction applies when the model emits a source code patch rather than an inspection request. A candidate patch can parse cleanly, compile against existing headers, and pass a sequential unit test while leaving the underlying race condition untouched. Each verification check answers a narrow, specific question rather than certifying overall task satisfaction. Robust candidate verification systems must track these separate dimensions of evidence explicitly rather than collapsing them into a single, undifferentiated notion of validity.

### Likelihood and checked properties {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-likelihood-checked-properties}

Autoregressive generation assigns probabilities based on patterns in training data and context tokens, reflecting linguistic familiarity rather than operational truth. Whether a generated path exists on disk, whether the caller holds read permissions, and whether an altered function preserves system invariants depend entirely on the operational environment and the task contract. An obsolete or nonexistent path often receives substantial model probability simply because it matches common directory conventions in the training corpus.

Sound verification begins by pairing each concrete property with the precise evidence required to validate it. For a `read_file` invocation, a schema validator checks that the payload contains only supported keys and provides a string-valued `path`. A passing result proves syntactic schema membership—assuming the validator implements the schema dialect faithfully and inspects the exact object forwarded to execution. Proving that the target file exists requires probing the filesystem, while establishing access rights requires evaluating the agent's current security grant against host operating system policies.

Static analysis and dynamic testing support fundamentally different operational claims. A compiler verifies type consistency and language constraints under fixed configuration flags, whereas a linter detects anti-patterns through static heuristic rules. Dynamic test suites execute concrete code paths and record runtime assertions. In the connection-pool scenario, a test that exercises single-threaded checkout and release operations provides zero empirical evidence regarding thread safety under concurrent contention. Even a repeatable, passing test verdict can leave critical execution paths completely unexercised.

Architecturally, these boundaries require the execution runtime to treat generated model output strictly as untrusted data rather than direct control flow. A candidate tool call remains passive data until an authorized tool handler ingests, verifies, and dispatches it. That handler enforces access boundaries at execution time,[^fn-complete-mediation-handler] completely independent of any self-assertions the model makes regarding its own permissions. Similarly, evaluating an untrusted patch requires running arbitrary machine instructions, demanding isolated execution sandboxes even during preliminary test runs.

[^fn-complete-mediation-handler]: **Complete Mediation**: One of the design principles that @saltzer1975 set out for protection systems: every access to every object is checked against current authority at the moment of access, not remembered from an earlier decision. The tool handler applies the same rule to a model's proposal, so a path validated when the request was composed is checked again when the read executes, closing the gap in which the grant or the file could have changed. \index{Complete mediation!tool handler}

### Self-review and external evidence {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-self-review-evidence}

Prompts that instruct a model to inspect or refine its own patch can surface shallow syntax errors or expose omitted edge cases. Crucially, however, model-based self-review is simply another autoregressive generation step sampled from the same parameter distribution and conditioned on the same incomplete context. When the generator operates under an incorrect assumption about an API or concurrency model, a self-review prompt typically reinforces that assumption rather than exposing it. Re-prompting does not create statistical independence. Empirical evaluations of self-correction without external grounding demonstrate this limit clearly: across complex reasoning tasks, models prompted to inspect their own answers rarely improve their accuracy and frequently introduce regressions [@huang2024cannot].

Engineers must maintain a firm conceptual separation between candidate refinement and formal property certification. A model-generated critique can guide iterative search, but deterministic external tools—compilers, linters, sandboxed test harnesses, and kernel access-control checks—must provide the definitive ground truth. No critique emitted by a model, whether self-generated or evaluated by an auxiliary judge model, carries the authority to validate a security boundary or approve deployment. When systems do employ learned judge models as secondary evaluators, their verdicts must be treated as noisy signals with measurable false-positive rates and known systematic biases, such as preferences for verbose explanations or specific candidate positions [@zheng2023judging].

A conditional-probability calculation clarifies why fallible verification gates leave residual risk. The following model parameters reflect a hypothetical scenario evaluating a candidate patch against a concurrency specification:

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-candidate-checker-posterior
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RESIDUAL DEFECT RATE AFTER A FALLIBLE CHECK (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-foundation-model-continuations, hypothetical checker case.
# │ Goal: Quantify defects among candidates receiving a passing verdict.
# │ Show: The conditional defect rate under explicitly assumed checker rates.
# │ How: Apply Bayes' rule; no independence assumption between repeated checks.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

class CandidateCheckerPosterior:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    defect_rate = 0.18  # hypothetical share violating the specified property
    false_accept_rate = 0.65  # hypothetical P(PASS | Defective)
    valid_accept_rate = 0.85  # hypothetical P(PASS | Valid)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    defective_pass = false_accept_rate * defect_rate
    valid_pass = valid_accept_rate * (1 - defect_rate)
    posterior = defective_pass / (defective_pass + valid_pass)
    catch_rate = 1 - false_accept_rate  # share of defective patches rejected
    valid_reject = 1 - valid_accept_rate  # share of valid patches rejected
    fa_half = false_accept_rate / 2  # sensitivity: a checker with half the false-accept rate
    posterior_half = (fa_half * defect_rate) / (fa_half * defect_rate + valid_pass)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(posterior - 0.1437346437346437) < 1e-12, "The assumed rates must leave about 14.37 percent defective passes")
    check(0 < posterior < defect_rate, "This checker reduces but does not eliminate the assumed defect rate")
    check(posterior_half < posterior / 1.5, "Halving false accepts must cut the residual substantially")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    defect_pct_str = fmt_percent(defect_rate, precision=0, style="prose")
    false_accept_str = fmt(false_accept_rate, precision=2, commas=False)
    valid_accept_str = fmt(valid_accept_rate, precision=2, commas=False)
    posterior_pct_str = fmt_percent(posterior, precision=2, style="prose")
    catch_pct_str = fmt_percent(catch_rate, precision=0, style="prose")
    valid_reject_pct_str = fmt_percent(valid_reject, precision=0, style="prose")
    fa_half_str = fmt(fa_half, precision=3, commas=False)
    posterior_half_pct_str = fmt_percent(posterior_half, precision=1, style="prose")
    substitution_math = fmt_math(
        rf"\frac{{{false_accept_rate} \times {defect_rate}}}"
        rf"{{({false_accept_rate} \times {defect_rate}) + "
        rf"({valid_accept_rate} \times (1 - {defect_rate}))}}"
        rf"\approx {posterior * 100:.2f}\%"
    )
```

::: {#psp-02-the-fallacy-of-correlated-self-verification .callout-perspective title="What a passing verdict leaves unresolved"}

Suppose `{python} CandidateCheckerPosterior.defect_pct_str` of generated patches violate a specified behavioral property. For this population, assume the checker passes defective patches with probability $\epsilon_{\text{FA}} =$ `{python} CandidateCheckerPosterior.false_accept_str` and passes valid patches with probability `{python} CandidateCheckerPosterior.valid_accept_str`. Let $\epsilon$ denote the defect rate and $\epsilon_{\text{FA}}$ the false-accept rate. Bayes' rule gives the fraction of defective patches among the passing results:

$$\Pr(\text{Defective} \mid \text{PASS}) = \frac{\epsilon_{\text{FA}} \cdot \epsilon}{\epsilon_{\text{FA}} \cdot \epsilon + \Pr(\text{PASS} \mid \text{Valid}) \cdot (1 - \epsilon)}$$

Substituting the assumed rates gives `{python} CandidateCheckerPosterior.substitution_math`. The defect share among passing patches falls only from `{python} CandidateCheckerPosterior.defect_pct_str` to `{python} CandidateCheckerPosterior.posterior_pct_str`, because the checker rejects `{python} CandidateCheckerPosterior.catch_pct_str` of defective patches while also rejecting `{python} CandidateCheckerPosterior.valid_reject_pct_str` of valid ones. The lever is $\epsilon_{\text{FA}}$: a checker with half the false-accept rate, `{python} CandidateCheckerPosterior.fa_half_str`, lowers the residual to `{python} CandidateCheckerPosterior.posterior_half_pct_str`. Repeating the same check buys no such guarantee, because its behavior on the surviving candidates is correlated with the first pass. Every defective patch that passes also inflates the apparent acceptance probability $p_{\text{acc}}$ in the cost per accepted task (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task).

A sound checker for the exact property drives $\epsilon_{\text{FA}}$ to zero under its assumptions. Determinism alone does not supply soundness, and soundness for schema membership does not extend to patch behavior. The verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}) underscores a primary design rule: select each validation gate based on the specific property it establishes and its false-accept rate, letting the task contract determine what residual defect rate the system can safely tolerate.

:::

### A pipeline of scoped checks {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-scoped-check-pipeline}

In production systems, executing full end-to-end integration tests or sandboxed reproduction scripts is orders of magnitude more expensive than parsing JSON or running a static linter. Consequently, the runtime organizes candidate verification into an ascending cascade, rejecting malformed or unauthorized requests early before spending compute on deep behavioral evaluation. Staging checks by cost optimizes throughput, but each gate validates an orthogonal property rather than an increasingly strict approximation of overall correctness. @Tbl-verification-layers categorizes these verification layers alongside their computational overhead and formal evidentiary boundaries.

| Verification layer        | Gate mechanism                                   | Property or evidence                                             | Cost to account for                            | Limit of the claim                                                |
|:--------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Syntax and schema**     | Parser and schema validator                      | Required fields, supported types, and declared value constraints | Parsing and validation                         | Does not establish permission or correct values beyond the schema |
| **Authorization**         | Task permission check and enforcing tool handler | Requested operation and target fall within the current grant     | Policy lookup and mediation                    | Permission does not establish that the operation serves the goal  |
| **Static analysis**       | Compiler, type checker, or linter                | Properties covered by the selected analysis and configuration    | Analysis of the candidate and its dependencies | Coverage depends on the checker and language assumptions          |
| **Behavioral evaluation** | Controlled execution and designated tests        | Observed outcomes for the exercised inputs and conditions        | Environment preparation and execution          | Passing cases do not establish untested behavior                  |
: **Scoped candidate checks**: A passing result supports a named claim, not every property needed for task acceptance. The runtime preserves these distinctions when composing the checks. {#tbl-verification-layers tbl-colwidths="[17,19,24,16,24]"}

Consider how this tiered pipeline evaluates an inspection request. Before dispatching `read_file`, the runtime verifies that the candidate stream completed normally, confirms that the argument payload conforms to schema types, and checks that the targeted path falls within current sandbox grants. Executing the read operation simply feeds environmental state back to the agent for subsequent reasoning cycles rather than completing the overall bug fix. Conversely, when evaluating a proposed patch, the pipeline validates patch syntax and file targets, applies the diff inside an isolated scratch workspace, and triggers targeted unit tests. Final acceptance adheres to the task contract's explicit evidentiary standard, escalating to human review when automated checks cannot decisively settle safety or correctness criteria.

Every stage in this pipeline assumes an explicit understanding of what the upstream model service returned. Standard parsers evaluate syntax in isolation; a JSON parser, for example, cannot distinguish between a fully formed response and a truncated string that happens to close its braces by coincidence. A passing check must never promote an interrupted generation into a verified candidate. Instead, the runtime relies on the model invocation contract—incorporating stop reasons, token length limits, and explicit finish metadata—to certify that a candidate sequence is genuinely complete before initiating downstream verification.
## The Invocation Contract {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract}

Suppose a model begins generating a cleanup command targeting the path `/tmp/scratch/cache_dir`, but reaches its token limit immediately after emitting `/tmp/scratch`. Both strings form syntactically valid shell commands, yet they specify vastly different deletion boundaries. An execution engine inspecting only raw text cannot determine whether the shorter path represents an intended command or a dangerously truncated prefix. To prevent catastrophic side effects, the host runtime requires an explicit execution outcome alongside the payload.

By pairing request specifications with normalized response envelopes at the invocation boundary, the runtime treats each remote generation as a unified contract.

::: {#dfn-vol3-model-invocation-contract .callout-definition title="Model invocation contract"}

***Model invocation contract***\index{Model invocation contract!definition} is the pair of records that bounds one model call: a request fixing the input, model configuration, sampling settings, and enforced output and time limits, and a normalized envelope reporting the call's status, payload, and resource use.

1.  **Significance**: The contract establishes each model call as a distinct, countable unit within an agent trajectory. Its usage record prices the call's share of $C_{\text{attempt}}$, and its status flag isolates completed generations from partial or failed calls. Consequently, the cost per accepted task (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task) can be computed from recorded telemetry rather than heuristically reconstructed from conversation transcripts.
2.  **Distinction**: The invocation contract describes the model call rather than the overarching task. A generated tool request can fully conform to decoding limits without ever being dispatched, and a fully generated response can fail downstream validation. Dispatch authorization, tool execution, and task-level acceptance remain separate runtime decisions backed by their own evidence.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Recording only the payload text. Without explicit status flags and usage accounting, a truncated fragment is indistinguishable from an intentional short response, and unrecorded token consumption silently distorts operational cost accounting as zero-cost execution.

:::

### Formal request specification {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-request-specification}

At the generation interface, the bounded request is represented by the tuple

$$\mathcal{R} = \langle \mathbf{x}, \text{ModelID}, K_{\max}, T_{\max}, \mathcal{S}_{\text{stop}}, \mathbf{\Theta}_{\text{sample}} \rangle$$

The prompt tokens $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_S)$ encode the serialized messages, role markers, advertised tool schemas, and formatting delimiters visible to the model. The runtime constructs this sequence from structured `messages` and `tools` configuration fields prior to serialization.

`ModelID` identifies the target model weights and serving deployment requested through `model_config`. Systems engineers must distinguish mutable provider aliases (such as `model-latest`) from immutable, pinned model revisions (such as content-addressed snapshots). The sampling parameters $\mathbf{\Theta}_{\text{sample}}$, including temperature and top-$p$, configure the stochastic selection rule applied during autoregressive decode. Together with the serialized input and returned output, the resolved configuration uniquely explains a call; exact regeneration also depends on backend serving implementation details, as war story \ref{ws-02-anthropic-serving-bugs-2025} demonstrated.

The resource limits specify an output allowance $K_{\max}$ and a local waiting deadline $T_{\max}$.
