Systems cannot rely on the model itself to halt generation gracefully; following the invariant closure principle (\ref{pri-invariant-closure}), the host runtime and the remote serving system must enforce these boundaries mechanically. The runtime verifies that the combined prompt and generation budget fits within the service engine's context window. In addition, the adapter records whether the provider charges non-visible reasoning tokens against $K_{\max}$, since measuring visible text length alone would understate actual resource consumption.

The stop sequences $\mathcal{S}_{\text{stop}}$ define token patterns that trigger an immediate halt at the serving interface. When an inference engine encounters a matching sequence, it stops decoding according to provider matching semantics. However, an engine matches byte sequences blindly: encountering a stop sequence inside an argument or quoted string can terminate generation before closing brackets or quotation marks are emitted. The host runtime must therefore record the provider's raw stop reason and validate candidate syntax independently.

Resource enforcement operates across two distinct physical boundaries: the client host and the remote serving cluster. On the host side, the runtime enforces a receive buffer limit on incoming bytes and a local deadline $T_{\max}$ on waiting time. An expired local deadline halts host waiting and marks the invocation as failed, but it provides no guarantee that the remote server has halted execution or freed GPU allocations.[^fn-rpc-unknown-outcome] Server-side token ceilings and cancellation protocols complement these client-side controls. Every operational limit must clearly specify which component enforces it and which physical resource it governs.

[^fn-rpc-unknown-outcome]: **Remote Call Semantics**: Remote procedure call designers met this ambiguity first. In the design @birrell1984rpc describe, a call that returns normally executed exactly once, but a call that ends in a failure report may have executed once or not at all, because the caller cannot tell a lost request from a lost reply. A model call inherits the same gap: a timed-out generation may still have run to completion and been billed, which is why `TRANSPORT_FAILURE` records an unknown remote outcome rather than a call that never happened. \index{Remote procedure call!unknown outcome}

### The normalized status envelope {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-status-envelope}

The runtime represents the observed outcome using the **normalized status envelope**\index{Normalized status envelope!definition}

$$\mathcal{N} = \langle \text{status}, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{m} \rangle$$

Here, $\mathbf{y}$ denotes the returned payload, which may be complete, partial, or absent. The metadata record $\mathbf{m}$ captures operational telemetry: the response `kind`, the raw provider `stop_reason`, reported token `usage`, unique request identifiers, latency measurements, and serving parameters. In concrete implementations, these attributes appear as fields on a response object; grouping them formally into a tuple decouples the raw text payload from the evidence documenting how it arrived. Unreported usage represents unmeasured cost rather than zero cost.

Because proprietary model APIs express termination conditions using divergent finish reasons, error codes, and transport exceptions, the adapter maps provider-specific signals onto the seven normalized statuses defined in @tbl-vol3-invocation-status. This taxonomy provides this book's normalized interface. A status flag records the outcome verified locally by the host runtime; when concurrent events race—such as a local cancellation overlapping with an incoming completion frame—the adapter applies deterministic resolution rules while preserving the raw provider signals in $\mathbf{m}$.

| Status flag         | Terminal condition                                                               | Payload integrity                                                              | Admissible host action                                               |
|:--------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `COMPLETED`         | Confirmed normal generation termination within the call's limits                 | Fully generated according to the protocol; syntax and meaning remain unchecked | Admit to candidate validation, not directly to dispatch              |
| `TRUNCATED`         | Generation reaches a token or context ceiling before confirmed normal completion | Incomplete candidate that may nevertheless parse                               | Withhold from action; record the limit and diagnose                  |
| `REFUSED`           | The model or service explicitly declines the request or response                 | Refusal notice, partial content, or no payload                                 | Handle under the task's refusal policy; do not treat as an action    |
| `TRANSPORT_FAILURE` | Delivery fails or the local deadline expires without accepted completion         | Missing or partial content; remote outcome may be unknown                      | Record uncertainty and apply bounded failure handling                |
| `REJECTED`          | A runtime monitor rejects the response during reception                          | Content observed before rejection                                              | Withhold from action; record the rejection and request cancellation  |
| `CANCELED`          | The runtime cancels the call before accepting its completion                     | Partial, missing, or otherwise unusable as a completed candidate               | Stop local candidate processing; track remote termination separately |
| `FAULTED`           | The service reports an execution failure                                         | Missing, partial, or diagnostic content                                        | Record the reported fault and route to failure handling              |
: **Normalized invocation status envelope**: Status controls admission to the candidate path. Completion is a generation outcome, while authorization, tool execution, and task acceptance remain separate decisions. {#tbl-vol3-invocation-status tbl-colwidths="[21,27,25,27]"}

For an artifact such as a `read_file` request, `kind="tool_request"` instructs the runtime which candidate representation to validate, while `status="COMPLETED"` confirms that generation finished under the interface contract. Neither field confirms that the host dispatched the tool or that the filesystem operation succeeded; completion tracks protocol generation, whereas execution and task acceptance remain separate host decisions.

Applying the invariant closure principle (\ref{pri-invariant-closure}) to the status field establishes a mandatory gate: the **quarantining rule**\index{Quarantining rule!definition}. Under this rule, any payload whose invocation envelope reports a status other than `COMPLETED` cannot pass into the candidate execution pipeline. The runtime must verify the status flag before admitting content to downstream parsing or action dispatch. While the system may inspect malformed or interrupted output inside an isolated diagnostic sandbox, that inspection cannot authorize tool dispatch or silently reclassify the fragment as a finished proposal. Search branches terminated by token limits must obey this same constraint. Under the quarantining rule, a truncated payload is treated as a diagnosable failure rather than a partial action.

The cleanup command introduced earlier demonstrates why structural parsing alone cannot replace this status check. Suppose the complete intended command is

```bash
rm -rf /tmp/scratch/cache_dir
```

If an exhausted token quota truncates generation midway through the path, the resulting prefix is

```bash
rm -rf /tmp/scratch
```

The truncated string parses as valid shell syntax, but it broadens the deletion scope to the entire parent directory. If the envelope marks this output as `TRUNCATED`, the quarantining rule holds the command in quarantine, preventing accidental execution. Conversely, receiving `status="COMPLETED"` does not grant execution authority; it merely establishes that the model finished generating its proposal. Neither command represents an approved cleanup policy on its own; the comparison underscores that syntactic validity cannot substitute for verified completion evidence.

Listing @Lst-vol3-completed-candidate-gate implements this admission check. The gate admits only completed generations to downstream processing, leaving syntax validation, permission checks, and task-level verification to subsequent stages.

::: {#lst-vol3-completed-candidate-gate lst-cap="**Completed-candidate admission**: The status check admits only completed generations to the candidate path. Returning the payload grants no execution authority."}
```python
def completed_candidate(envelope):
    if envelope["status"] != "COMPLETED":
        raise ValueError("Response is not a completed candidate")
    # Syntax, permission, and task evidence remain unchecked.
    return envelope["payload"]
```
:::

Incomplete payloads are redirected to a dedicated diagnostic log governed by its own memory and access bounds. This log retains the partial byte stream alongside the observed `stop_reason` to assist failure analysis. Attempting to "repair" a truncated fragment by appending guessed arguments or synthetic delimiters produces an entirely new candidate devoid of generation provenance; such synthetic patches can never inherit the `COMPLETED` status of the original call.

### Streaming and cancellation {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-streaming-cancellation}

**Streaming**\index{Streaming!definition} delivers incremental response fragments across an active network connection before generation finishes. A delivery chunk can contain part of a decoded sub-word, several tokens, or an application-layer framing event. The host runtime must adhere to the provider's framing protocol rather than assuming a one-to-one correspondence between chunks and tokens. Incremental inspection allows the runtime to discover early structural violations; if a prefix violates format constraints, the monitor halts waiting immediately rather than buffering unusable tokens. Because generation is ongoing, the monitor evaluates whether the prefix can transition to a valid completion, rather than testing whether the prefix is already complete.

Rejection and cancellation represent distinct operational events. When an incremental monitor detects a structural violation, the host runtime sets the call status to `REJECTED` and issues a cancellation signal to the remote endpoint. If an operator or client-side timeout interrupts an otherwise compliant response, the runtime marks the status as `CANCELED`. In both scenarios, withholding the partial payload from tool dispatch is an invariant the host enforces locally. However, halting remote decode loops and reclaiming GPU memory require the serving engine to process and honor the cancellation request. Simply closing a TCP socket provides no guarantee that remote execution has ceased.

```{python}
#| label: lego-stream-cancel
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ GENERATION WORK SPARED BY EARLY CANCELLATION (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract, streaming and cancellation;
# │          @fig-vol3-streaming-cancellation.
# │ Goal: Bound the decode work a honored cancel request can avoid.
# │ Show: 4,000 skipped decode steps; their time at the reference output floor.
# │ How: (K_max - t_cut) steps times the weight-transfer floor per output token,
# │      the same floor that CallPrice uses in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_INT8
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_count, fmt_time

class StreamCancel:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    accel = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    weight_bytes = BYTES_INT8
    k_cap = 4_096  # scenario: output allowance of the canceled call (as drawn in the figure)
    k_cut = 96  # scenario: decode step at which the stream monitor rejects (as drawn)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_dec = ((model.parameters / ureg.param * weight_bytes) / accel.memory.bandwidth).to(second)
    cancel_steps = k_cap - k_cut
    cancel_s = cancel_steps * t_dec

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(cancel_steps == 4_000, "The figure labels 4,000 decode steps not run")
    check(cancel_s > 10 * second, "Early cancellation should spare tens of seconds of decode")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    k_cap_str = fmt_count(k_cap)
    k_cut_str = fmt_count(k_cut)
    cancel_steps_str = fmt_count(cancel_steps)
    t_dec_ms_str = fmt_time(t_dec, unit=ms, precision=3)
    cancel_s_str = fmt_time(cancel_s, unit=second, precision=1)
```

@Fig-vol3-streaming-cancellation illustrates this control sequence for an invocation configured with an output allowance of `{python} StreamCancel.k_cap_str` tokens. At decode step $t_{\text{cut}} =$ `{python} StreamCancel.k_cut_str`, the generated proposal introduces a key disallowed by the schema. The runtime stream monitor immediately rejects the response, records `REJECTED`, and dispatches a cancellation signal to the serving backend.

::: {#fig-vol3-streaming-cancellation fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Reject, Then Cancel**: The runtime's stream validator advances a parser state as each prefix arrives and holds the output rather than acting on it. At step `{python} StreamCancel.k_cut_str` the proposal introduces a key outside the schema, so the runtime records a rejection, discards the partial proposal, and sends a cancel request. The runtime outcomes on the left hold regardless of the service; the service outcomes on the right hold only if the service receives and honors the cancel request." fig-alt="Sequence diagram with an agent runtime lane on the left, a token stream lane in the middle, and a model service lane on the right. Decode steps 1 and 2 deliver an opening brace and a query key, each accepted by a parser transition and held. Steps 3 to 95 continue. Decode step 96 delivers a force key, and the runtime marks the stream rejected with status REJECTED, discards the partial proposal, and sends a cancel request; the service lane shows decoding stopping at step 96 of up to 4,096. Summary boxes list runtime outcomes, partial proposal never dispatched, rejection recorded, error returned next turn, and service outcomes, labeled as holding only if the cancel is honored: up to 4,000 decode steps not run, request leaves the batch, KV cache memory released."}
![](images/svg/streaming_token_cancellation.svg)
:::

The compute savings shown represent an upper bound that requires provider cooperation. If the serving engine processes the cancellation promptly, it skips up to $K_{\max} - t_{\text{cut}} =$ `{python} StreamCancel.cancel_steps_str` autoregressive decode steps. At the baseline memory-bandwidth decode floor of `{python} StreamCancel.t_dec_ms_str` per generated token modeled in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost, avoiding these steps recovers up to `{python} StreamCancel.cancel_s_str` of GPU compute time, frees slots in the continuous batching scheduler, and releases the call's KV-cache allocations. If the remote service fails to honor the cancellation, the host runtime still quarantines the rejected payload locally, but the remote cluster consumes its entire token allowance.

Nonstreaming invocations enforce the exact same candidate admission barrier at batch completion. Streaming shifts the observation boundary earlier in the call lifecycle, enabling rapid rejection and resource recovery without relaxing the rule that incomplete prefixes must never trigger external side effects. While constrained decoding and formal grammars can eliminate syntax errors during generation, the host runtime must always maintain the distinction between an acceptable partial prefix and a validated, completed candidate.
## Grammar-Guided Decoding {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-grammar-constrained}

Consider a software repair agent attempting to inspect an unfamiliar module by calling `read_file(path)` with argument `"src/pool.py"`. If the model's generated text omits the closing quotation mark before emitting an end-of-turn token, the runtime parser encounters malformed JSON and rejects the payload before dispatching the call. That parser check successfully shields the execution boundary from syntactic corruption, yet resolving the failure demands another full autoregressive generation pass. Retrying a failed call consumes additional latency—often several hundred milliseconds or more—wastes GPU inference budget, and risks introducing secondary errors. When the system knows the target output structure ahead of time, the inference engine can proactively eliminate tokens that violate the required syntax during generation, preventing structural defects before they reach the tool boundary.

::: {#dfn-grammar-constrained-decoding .callout-definition title="Grammar-constrained decoding"}

***Grammar-constrained decoding***\index{Grammar-constrained decoding!definition}\index{Logit masking!definition} restricts next-token selection during autoregressive generation to tokens whose decoded text preserves a viable prefix of a target formal grammar.

1. **Significance**: Dynamic token masking guarantees that any completed generation sequence strictly satisfies the structural grammar, eliminating syntax errors at the model boundary when the constraint parser covers the target schema.
2. **Distinction**: Post-generation validation inspects an already emitted sequence and discards invalid payloads after full generation. Constrained decoding actively shapes the vocabulary distribution at every generation step. Even so, neither approach verifies whether a syntactically correct payload contains sensible parameter values or possesses valid execution permissions.
3. **Common pitfall**: Mistaking a viable prefix for a completed data structure. If token limits, request timeouts, or connection failures truncate generation early, the emitted sequence remains an unfinished prefix that cannot be safely dispatched.

:::

### Legal prefixes and completed structures {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-legal-prefixes}

The constraint engine maintains a running parse state synchronized with the sequence generated so far. Consider a schema expecting a string-valued `path` parameter. Once the prefix `{"path":` appears in the decoding buffer, the grammar allows optional whitespace followed by an opening quotation mark, but forbids unquoted booleans, numbers, or bare identifiers. When the generator emits `{"path":"src/`, the text represents a viable prefix:[^fn-viable-prefix-lr] while incomplete as a JSON document, it can still transition into a valid object through subsequent string and delimiter tokens. The fundamental mechanism of constrained decoding relies on evaluating whether a candidate token can extend the current prefix toward an accepting grammar state.

[^fn-viable-prefix-lr]: **Legal (Viable) Prefix**: The viable-prefix concept stems from classical compiler theory. The LR parsers introduced by @knuth1965translation read input strings left to right, identifying an error at the exact first symbol that cannot extend the sequence into any valid sentence of the language. A grammar mask applies this principle constructively: instead of catching syntax violations after generation finishes, the engine prunes invalid transition tokens from the vocabulary before sampling. \index{Viable prefix!grammar-constrained decoding}

At generation step $t$, let $q_t$ represent the parser's internal state, including nested scope tracking for recursive structures. Let $\mathcal{V}_{\text{valid}}(q_t)$ denote the set of vocabulary tokens whose decoded strings maintain a viable prefix under the target grammar. Because modern language models operate on subword tokens rather than individual characters, a single token can span multiple characters, punctuation marks, or whitespace segments (for example, `", "limit": 10}` or `true`). The engine must therefore simulate the parser across the token's full decoded byte sequence to confirm that every character transition is valid.

Incremental parsing demonstrates that pruning invalid tokens at each decoding step produces syntactically flawless outputs for domain-specific languages such as SQL [@scholak2021picard]. To minimize per-step latency, guided-generation frameworks precompute transition tables between the target grammar and the model vocabulary, converting the valid-token search into an efficient table lookup during the forward pass [@willard2023outlines].

For each token index $i$ in vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$, the constraint engine constructs an additive logit mask:

$$M_i(q_t) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i \in \mathcal{V}_{\text{valid}}(q_t) \\ -\infty & \text{if } i \notin \mathcal{V}_{\text{valid}}(q_t) \end{cases}$$

Adding this mask to the unnormalized logit vector $\mathbf{z}_t$ produces the filtered logit vector $\mathbf{z}_t' = \mathbf{z}_t + \mathbf{M}(q_t)$. At unit temperature, the resulting softmax distribution becomes

$$p_{t, i} = \frac{\exp(z_{t, i}')}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{V}} \exp(z_{t, j}')} = \begin{cases} \frac{\exp(z_{t, i})}{\sum_{k \in \mathcal{V}_{\text{valid}}(q_t)} \exp(z_{t, k})} & \text{if } i \in \mathcal{V}_{\text{valid}}(q_t) \\ 0 & \text{if } i \notin \mathcal{V}_{\text{valid}}(q_t) \end{cases}$$

Setting the logits of invalid tokens to $-\infty$ forces their sampling probabilities to zero, renormalizing the distribution entirely across viable continuations. Once the sampler draws a token from this restricted set, the engine consumes that token's characters and advances the parser to state $q_{t+1}$. This formulation assumes that $\mathcal{V}_{\text{valid}}(q_t)$ remains nonempty and that the sampling configuration respects the mask. If aggressive top-$k$ truncation or temperature filtering eliminates all elements of $\mathcal{V}_{\text{valid}}(q_t)$, the serving runtime must raise an explicit constraint-satisfaction error rather than silently disabling the mask.

@Fig-vol3-grammar-constrained-fsm arranges this loop into three stages: compile the schema once, mask the logits at every step, then sample and advance the parser state.

::: {#fig-vol3-grammar-constrained-fsm fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Grammar-Constrained Decoding**: A tool schema compiles once into an automaton whose states each carry a token mask. At every step the mask sets illegal tokens to $-\infty$ before normalization, so only a legal continuation can be drawn, and the drawn token advances the automaton. The logit values are illustrative: a fluent but illegal continuation can outscore the legal one and still receive zero probability. A precomputed per-state mask suits a finite-state constraint; nested structures need additional parser state. The last panel lists what the mask leaves unchecked." fig-alt="Three-panel diagram. Panel 1, compile the tool schema: a JSON argument schema with query and limit fields, an automaton with states q_0, q_1, q_2, and final state q_F, and per-state bitmasks B of q. Panel 2, mask the logits: four candidate tokens SELECT, I think, opening brace, and Sure with illustrative scores, three marked masked and the opening brace allowed, and a note that masked tokens get zero probability. Panel 3, sample and advance: the emitted token is the opening brace, the automaton moves from q_0 to q_1, the next legal tokens are query and limit, and a box lists what the mask does not check: whether the table exists, whether the values are right, and whether the call is authorized."}
![](images/svg/grammar_constrained_decoding_fsm.svg)
:::

Generating viable prefixes guarantees that the output will not contain invalid syntax, but it does not guarantee that generation finishes cleanly. For the output to form a complete, usable payload, two operational conditions must hold: the parser must reach an accepting state, and the generation sequence must terminate according to the protocol rules. The constraint engine must disallow end-of-sequence (`<eos>`) tokens whenever required fields or closing delimiters remain unwritten. As a result, maintaining viable prefixes provides a conditional guarantee: completed outputs are structurally sound, but the system cannot assume that every generation request finishes within its allocated token budget. @Sec-vol3-appendix-math-dfa formalizes these token-to-parser state transitions and details the formal proof for accepting-state termination.

Consider what happens when an inference request hits its maximum output token limit while emitting arguments, leaving the decoding buffer at `{"path":"src/po`. Although this string remains a viable prefix under the schema, the inference service flags the response envelope with `status: TRUNCATED`. The payload contains only an incomplete fragment. The agent runtime cannot dispatch this fragment as a valid `tool_request`. Furthermore, attempting to "heal" the payload by running a heuristic repair parser that appends closing quotes and braces creates severe reliability hazards. Heuristic completion fabricates a candidate invocation (`"src/po"`) that the model never intended to finalize, risking unintended execution side effects. The runtime should log the truncated fragment for debugging under status-first handling, but grammar constraints do not bypass the fundamental requirement to quarantine incomplete artifacts (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}).

### Scope of the structural guarantee {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-structural-guarantee-scope}

A payload can adhere to every syntactic rule in a schema while remaining completely incorrect in practice. In our file-reading scenario, an output such as `{"path":"src/pool.py"}` provides the required key and string type, yet the specified file might not exist in the repository, its contents might be unreadable, or the agent might lack permissions to access the path. Grammar masking operates strictly on the textual representation; it does not query repository state, check system dependencies, or validate security policies. @Tbl-vol3-verification-dimensions delineates the distinct verification boundaries that a system must satisfy before treating a generated proposal as safe, executable work.

| Verification dimension    | Governed by grammar mask?                              | Required check or evidence                                    | What remains unestablished              |
|:--------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------|
| **Syntactic conformance** | Yes, for the enforced grammar                          | Complete text accepted under that grammar                     | Correct field values                    |
| **Schema completeness**   | Only for supported constraints at accepting completion | Required fields, types, and encoded restrictions              | Completion before a token or time limit |
| **Referential integrity** | Not from a structural schema alone                     | Observation of the named resource in the relevant environment | Permission to use that resource         |
| **Semantic invariants**   | Not from structural validity alone                     | Checks or judgments covering the task property                | Correctness beyond their coverage       |
| **Authorization bounds**  | No authority is granted by generated text              | Runtime permission decision for the proposed operation        | Successful execution or task acceptance |
: **Verification dimension boundaries**: A completed constrained output can establish membership in the enforced output language. The remaining claims require their own checks and evidence. {#tbl-vol3-verification-dimensions tbl-colwidths="[20,24,29,27]"}

The strength of the structural guarantee depends directly on the formal expressive power of the enforced grammar. Enforcing a general JSON grammar guarantees only that the output obeys RFC 8259 syntax—balanced braces, legal numeric formats, and escaped strings—without constraining object keys or data types. In contrast, compiling a specific JSON Schema into the constraint engine allows the runtime to enforce required properties, restrict types (such as distinguishing floating-point numbers from integers), and constrain string values to specific regular expressions or enumerations.

Engineering challenges arise when a schema relies on advanced features that the constraint compiler cannot translate into finite-state or pushdown automata. For example, schema keywords enforcing cross-field conditional dependencies (`if`/`then`/`else`), unique array elements, or complex lookahead assertions often exceed the capabilities of precomputed token masks. If an execution engine encounters unsupported schema features, an improper grammar compiler, or divergent type interpretations between the generator and consumer, the structural guarantee collapses. To maintain system integrity, the runtime must document which schema features its engine enforces and perform a final validation pass against its authoritative interface before dispatch. Logit masking acts as a mechanical filter situated below the model in the hierarchy of invariant closure (\ref{pri-invariant-closure}): it guarantees syntactic conformance without requiring model cooperation, leaving semantic acceptance and authorization to verification layers situated above the model.

Schema structure directly influences how an agent handles ambiguity or missing context. When a schema strictly mandates a file path with no alternative representations, every accepted completion must provide a path string—even when the prompt context provides no reasonable clue about which file to inspect. By stripping away all tokens outside the target structure, an over-constrained mask removes the agent's ability to communicate that critical information is missing. Under these conditions, the model has no choice but to invent a plausible file path to reach an accepting parser state.

Systems engineers can prevent this forced confabulation by designing schemas that incorporate explicit fallback variants, such as an `unknown` payload variant or a structured `error` field. Providing an `unknown` branch allows the agent to signal insufficient information directly within the schema without inventing fictitious data. These variants represent distinct semantic branches within the model's output payload; they should not be confused with transport-level invocation statuses or runtime tool execution failures.

Engineers must also recognize that introducing fallback branches does not prevent semantic misuse. An agent might still output a fabricated file path when an `unknown` variant is available, or falsely trigger an error state when sufficient context exists. The execution runtime must evaluate each payload variant according to the application's task contract, gathering targeted observations or asking for user clarification when uncertainty arises. The schema provides the expressiveness necessary for honest reporting; external system observations determine whether the agent's reported choice is justified.

### Learned formatting and runtime constraints {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-learned-formatting-constraints}

Supervised fine-tuning and targeted instruction tuning teach models to associate natural language prompts with specific tool definitions, biasing generation toward well-structured function arguments [@schick2023toolformer]. Runtime logit masking operates at a different systems layer: it determines the exact mathematical support of the vocabulary distribution at each generation step. Learned formatting shifts probability mass toward expected syntax, while masking reduces the probability of every illegal token strictly to zero. These two strategies reinforce each other. A model tuned for structured calling reliably allocates high logits to semantically appropriate tokens, while the runtime mask guarantees that subtle sampling variations or long-context degradations cannot produce malformed syntax.

Neither approach substitutes for the other. Statistical alignment alone yields no formal guarantee against syntax violations, while a grammar mask contributes zero domain knowledge toward selecting the correct file path. The overall reliability of the agent depends on the synergy between training fidelity, expressive schema definitions, and robust runtime constraints.

Furthermore, deploying grammar constraints introduces concrete systems trade-offs that engineers must measure across the end-to-end request lifecycle. Compiling complex regular expressions or nested JSON schemas into deterministic automata consumes CPU time and memory. In dynamic environments where agents construct ad hoc schemas per request, compilation latency—frequently spanning 10 ms to 50 ms—can offset the latency saved by avoiding syntax retries. Similarly, tracking parse states and computing masks across large vocabularies ($|\mathcal{V}| \ge 128{,}000$ tokens) adds per-token decoding overhead unless supported by precomputed lookup indices or GPU-accelerated bitmasks. A systems engineer must evaluate compilation cost, serving memory footprint, and decoding throughput together, rather than assuming that eliminating syntax retries automatically reduces total operational cost.

::: {#chk-02-schema-constrained-decoding .callout-checkpoint title="Evaluating schema-constrained decoding"}

A repair agent uses constrained decoding for file-reading proposals. Its runtime records response kind and invocation status separately.

- [ ] **Completion**: If an output ceiling interrupts a legal JSON prefix, can you explain why grammar masking does not permit dispatch of the fragment?
- [ ] **Constraint scope**: If a completed request satisfies the schema but names a nonexistent file, can you identify which property was enforced and which observation is still needed?
- [ ] **Response variants**: A completed, schema-valid response selects the `unknown` variant. Decide what the runtime does next, and name the observation it should obtain before calling the model again.
- [ ] **Combined mechanisms**: Can you explain why a model trained for tool use can still benefit from runtime masks without either mechanism granting execution authority?

:::

Constrained decoding eliminates an entire class of syntax failures before dispatch, but a structurally valid invocation still requires sufficient compute budget to reach completion and external empirical evidence to justify execution. An agent architecture must account for schema compilation, input prompt processing, and token generation as distinct latency and cost factors. Balancing these overheads against the risk of unconstrained retries determines whether grammar-guided decoding delivers a net performance and reliability gain for a given task.
## The Cost of a Model Call {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost}

When an automated repair agent requests a code fix, it can ask the model for a localized diff or for the entire modified file. Both formats describe the same underlying patch, but the full-file approach forces the model to regenerate hundreds of lines of unchanged syntax alongside the edit. The runtime absorbs the latency and compute cost of generating those redundant tokens long before a compiler or test runner can validate the candidate patch. An effective invocation contract must therefore budget prompt reading and output writing explicitly, rather than treating every model invocation as a uniform, black-box unit of work.

Input length and output length stress distinct subsystems in the inference serving stack. Prompt ingestion exposes many known token positions to parallel matrix computation across the accelerator's execution units. Conversely, autoregressive token generation executes as a strictly sequential loop, where each new token depends on the hidden state of all preceding positions. Because hardware architectures handle these two phases under vastly different physical constraints, output length serves as the primary software lever for controlling generation latency. However, an excessively large prompt, an undersized reply, or a congested service queue can quickly shift the latency bottleneck elsewhere.

### Call latency decomposition {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-call-latency-decomposition}

From the perspective of an agent runtime, a model invocation begins when the runtime prepares the outbound request and ends when the normalized response is ready for dispatch to a tool or validation check. Within this end-to-end boundary, preparation spans local context assembly, payload serialization, and network dispatch; queueing measures the idle wait in the serving system's admission queue; **prefill**\index{Prefill!definition} processes the supplied prompt tokens in a single parallel forward pass; **decode**\index{Decode!definition} generates completion tokens through an autoregressive sequence of forward passes; and postprocessing encompasses network response transfer, wire deserialization, and schema validation. A non-overlapping accounting of these phases yields

$$T_{\text{call}} = T_{\text{prep}} + T_{\text{queue}} + T_{\text{prefill}} + T_{\text{decode}} + T_{\text{post}}$$ {#eq-vol3-call-latency}

Each term in @eq-vol3-call-latency represents an elapsed duration in seconds, captured via high-resolution timestamps rather than derived backward from token counts. When preparation or network transfer overlaps with server-side execution, telemetry spans must track concurrent execution explicitly to avoid double-counting. An agent runtime that instruments only aggregate wall-clock duration cannot diagnose whether an unexpected latency spike stems from a bloated prompt, a saturated inference queue, or an excessively verbose generation—even though each failure demands a fundamentally different architectural fix.

Accounting for the first generated token requires special care. In a standard Transformer architecture, the prefill pass processes the entire prompt and produces the initial logit distribution from which the first output token is sampled. From the client's perspective, the elapsed time between dispatching the request and receiving that initial token constitutes the **time to first token** (TTFT)\index{Time to first token!definition}, whereas the average delay between subsequent tokens defines the **time per output token** (TPOT)\index{Time per output token!definition}. Production serving systems treat TTFT and TPOT as separate service-level objectives because prefill and decode compete directly for shared accelerator compute and memory bandwidth. Indeed, disaggregated serving architectures separate prefill and decode onto physically distinct GPU worker pools to isolate these workloads and meet each objective independently [@zhong2024distserve].

When telemetry includes the sampling and transmission of the first token in TTFT, the remaining decode phase accounts for only the subsequent $K-1$ tokens in a completion of total length $K$. For a streamed response, adding client-measured TTFT, the inter-token arrival intervals across the remaining $K-1$ tokens, and trailing response deserialization captures total call latency without charging the first token twice. Notice that client-observed TTFT differs substantially from server-side prefill execution time because it also absorbs network transit and queueing delay. Furthermore, because network transports and serving runtimes frequently batch streamed tokens into multi-token network chunks, observed chunk-arrival intervals do not always reflect raw token-generation intervals on the accelerator.

Setting an output token limit caps generation volume rather than execution speed; an overloaded inference queue can easily consume an agent's entire timeout budget before prefill even completes. Meaningful latency benchmarks must therefore explicitly record the model architecture, prompt and completion lengths, prefix-cache conditions, and cluster load. Crucially, even when an agent executes single-threaded, sequential turns, the underlying serving system rarely processes that agent in isolation. Modern inference engines employ continuous batching to schedule, admit, and retire individual requests at the granularity of single token-generation steps [@yu2022orca], interleaving the agent's decode steps with requests from dozens of other concurrent clients.

### Per-call work estimate {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-per-call-work-estimate}

```{python}
#| label: lego-call-price
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CALL AND TRAJECTORY WORK ESTIMATES (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost and
# │          @sec-vol3-foundation-model-interface-design.
# │ Goal: Compare output volumes and repeated prompt processing under one
# │       explicit reference scenario, not predict measured service latency.
# │ Show: Per-call allowances, append-only resend arithmetic, prefix reuse,
# │       and whole-file versus localized-edit estimates at one task budget.
# │ How: Registry inference FLOPs / peak FP8 throughput gives the input
# │      allowance; registry weight bytes / bandwidth gives the output
# │      allowance. Neither includes attention, queueing, or serving overhead.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_INT8
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_count, fmt_math, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_time

class CallPrice:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    accel = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    agent = Agents.Coding.SWE_Bench_Runner
    weight_bytes = BYTES_INT8
    s0 = 8_000  # scenario: initial serialized prompt tokens
    delta = 1_500  # scenario: appended model output plus tool-observation tokens
    k_turn = 200  # scenario: output tokens per turn
    turns = agent.max_trajectory_steps
    k_full = 1_850  # scenario: whole-file response tokens
    k_diff = 80  # scenario: localized-edit response tokens
    dm_full = 350  # scenario: additional whole-file format instruction tokens
    dm_diff = 120  # scenario: additional localized-edit instruction tokens
    deadline = 15.0 * second  # scenario: call deadline
    syntax_ok = 0.95  # hypothetical fraction of localized edits that apply
    fix_rate = 0.60  # hypothetical test-pass fraction conditional on applying

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weights = model.parameters / ureg.param * weight_bytes
    t_dec = (weights / accel.memory.bandwidth).to(second)
    t_pre = (model.inference_flops / accel.compute.precision_flops["fp8"]).to(second)
    call1_pre = s0 * t_pre
    call1_dec = k_turn * t_dec
    call1_total = call1_pre + call1_dec
    sent_nocache = turns * s0 + delta * turns * (turns - 1) // 2
    # Reuse earlier PROMPT prefixes only; reprocess the whole appended suffix.
    sent_cache = s0 + delta * (turns - 1)
    out_total = turns * k_turn
    cache_saving = sent_nocache / sent_cache
    input_share = sent_nocache / (sent_nocache + out_total)
    pre_nocache = sent_nocache * t_pre
    pre_cache = sent_cache * t_pre
    dec_total = out_total * t_dec
    t_full = (s0 + dm_full) * t_pre + k_full * t_dec
    t_diff = (s0 + dm_diff) * t_pre + k_diff * t_dec
    speedup = t_full / t_diff
    pass_diff = syntax_ok * fix_rate
    ratio = (t_dec / t_pre).to("").magnitude
    ratio_closed = (accel.compute.precision_flops["fp8"] * weight_bytes / (2 * ureg.flop * accel.memory.bandwidth)).to("").magnitude
    call1_out_share = (call1_dec / call1_total).to("").magnitude  # output share of first-turn work
    call1_tok_share = k_turn / (s0 + k_turn)  # output share of first-turn tokens
    full_out_share = (k_full * t_dec / t_full).to("").magnitude  # output share of whole-file work
    deadline_margin = (deadline / t_diff).to("").magnitude
    turns_2x = 2 * turns  # sensitivity: doubled horizon
    sent_nocache_2x = turns_2x * s0 + delta * turns_2x * (turns_2x - 1) // 2
    sent_cache_2x = s0 + delta * (turns_2x - 1)
    growth_nocache = sent_nocache_2x / sent_nocache
    growth_cache = sent_cache_2x / sent_cache
    turns_3x = 3 * turns  # checkpoint horizon (answer left to the reader)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(t_pre > 0 * second and t_dec > 0 * second, "Positive work allowances")
    check(call1_dec > call1_pre, "Output dominates this first-turn estimate")
    check(ratio > 100, f"Decode floor should exceed prefill floor by two orders of magnitude, got {ratio:.0f}")
    check(abs(ratio - ratio_closed) / ratio < 0.01, "Ratio must match pi*b/(2*beta), as in the appendix")
    check(abs((t_dec - StreamCancel.t_dec).to(second).magnitude) < 1e-12, "Cancellation uses the same output floor")
    check(sent_nocache >= sent_cache >= s0, "Prefix reuse cannot add prefill work")
    check(input_share > 0.95, "Input dominates this scenario's token count")
    check(t_full > deadline > t_diff, "Scenario estimates straddle the deadline")
    check(0 <= pass_diff <= syntax_ok <= 1, "Conditional success is a fraction")
    check(call1_out_share > 0.8 and call1_tok_share < 0.05, "Output dominates first-turn work but not its tokens")
    check(full_out_share > 0.95, "Whole-file work is almost all generation")
    check(growth_nocache > 3 and growth_cache < 2, "Reuse turns quadratic growth near-linear")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    params_str = fmt_count(model.parameters, scale="B", precision=1)
    t_pre_us_str = fmt_time(t_pre, unit=microsecond, precision=2)
    t_dec_ms_str = fmt_time(t_dec, unit=ms, precision=3)
    ratio_str = fmt_int(ratio)
    s0_str = fmt_count(s0)
    delta_str = fmt_count(delta)
    k_turn_str = fmt_count(k_turn)
    turns_str = fmt_count(turns)
    call1_pre_str = fmt_time(call1_pre, unit=second, precision=3)
    call1_dec_str = fmt_time(call1_dec, unit=second, precision=3)
    call1_total_str = fmt_time(call1_total, unit=second, precision=3)
    input_share_str = fmt_percent(input_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    cache_saving_mult_str = fmt_multiple(cache_saving, precision=1)
    pre_nocache_str = fmt_time(pre_nocache, unit=second, precision=2)
    pre_cache_str = fmt_time(pre_cache, unit=second, precision=2)
    dec_total_str = fmt_time(dec_total, unit=second, precision=2)
    k_full_str = fmt_count(k_full)
    k_diff_str = fmt_count(k_diff)
    dm_full_str = fmt_count(dm_full)
    dm_diff_str = fmt_count(dm_diff)
    deadline_str = fmt_time(deadline, unit=second, precision=0)
    speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(speedup, precision=1)
    syntax_ok_pct_str = fmt_percent(syntax_ok, precision=0, style="prose")
    fix_rate_pct_str = fmt_percent(fix_rate, precision=0, style="prose")
    pass_diff_pct_str = fmt_percent(pass_diff, precision=0, style="prose")
    resend_math = fmt_math(rf"{turns}\times {s0:,}+{delta:,}\times\frac{{{turns}\times {turns-1}}}{{2}}={sent_nocache:,}")
    output_math = fmt_math(rf"{turns}\times {k_turn}={out_total:,}")
    cached_math = fmt_math(rf"{s0:,}+{turns-1}\times {delta:,}={sent_cache:,}")
    t_full_math = fmt_math(
        rf"({s0:,}+{dm_full})\times {t_pre.to(second).magnitude:.8f}\,\mathrm{{s}}+{k_full:,}\times {t_dec.to(second).magnitude:.6f}\,\mathrm{{s}}\approx {t_full.to(second).magnitude:.2f}\,\mathrm{{s}}"
    )
    t_diff_math = fmt_math(
        rf"({s0:,}+{dm_diff})\times {t_pre.to(second).magnitude:.8f}\,\mathrm{{s}}+{k_diff}\times {t_dec.to(second).magnitude:.6f}\,\mathrm{{s}}\approx {t_diff.to(second).magnitude:.2f}\,\mathrm{{s}}"
    )
    pass_diff_math = fmt_math(rf"{syntax_ok:.2f}\times {fix_rate:.2f}={pass_diff:.2f}")
    call1_out_pct_str = fmt_percent(call1_out_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    call1_tok_pct_str = fmt_percent(call1_tok_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    full_out_pct_str = fmt_percent(full_out_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    t_full_str = fmt_time(t_full, unit=second, precision=1)
    t_diff_str = fmt_time(t_diff, unit=second, precision=1)
    deadline_margin_mult_str = fmt_multiple(deadline_margin, precision=1)
    turns_2x_str = fmt_count(turns_2x)
    turns_3x_str = fmt_count(turns_3x)
    growth_nocache_mult_str = fmt_multiple(growth_nocache, precision=1)
    growth_cache_mult_str = fmt_multiple(growth_cache, precision=1)
```

To establish a baseline analytical model of per-call execution, we separate the computational allowance for input processing from the allowance for output generation, because fundamentally different physical hardware constraints govern the two phases. A standard dense Transformer model with $P$ parameters executes approximately $2P$ floating-point operations per token. During prompt prefill, the accelerator reads each weight tensor from high-bandwidth memory once and reuses those weights across all $S$ prompt positions simultaneously. A sufficiently long prompt amortizes memory transfers and pushes accelerator execution close to its peak arithmetic throughput $R_{\text{peak}}$. In contrast, standard single-stream decode generates only one token per step. Each step must stream the entire weight payload of $P b$ bytes (where $b$ denotes bytes per parameter) from high-bandwidth memory across the device memory bus $\text{BW}$. These dual regimes represent the compute ceiling and the memory-bandwidth slope of the roofline model [@williams2009]; empirical evaluations of Transformer inference confirm that prompt ingestion is typically compute-bound, whereas low-batch generation is intensely memory-bandwidth bound [@pope2023efficiently]:

$$t_{\text{prefill}} \approx \frac{2P}{R_{\text{peak}}}, \qquad t_{\text{decode}} \ge \frac{P b}{\text{BW}}$$ {#eq-vol3-fm-token-floors}

Dividing the two execution floors cancels the parameter count $P$:

$$\frac{t_{\text{decode}}}{t_{\text{prefill}}} \approx \frac{R_{\text{peak}} \, b}{2 \, \text{BW}}$$ {#eq-vol3-fm-floor-ratio}

Consider a concrete reference deployment: a dense model with `{python} CallPrice.params_str` parameters stored in 8-bit precision on a single accelerator. Evaluating @eq-vol3-fm-token-floors yields an input allowance of `{python} CallPrice.t_pre_us_str` per prompt token and an output allowance of `{python} CallPrice.t_dec_ms_str` per generated token. Under @eq-vol3-fm-floor-ratio, decoding a single output token requires the same hardware execution time as ingesting roughly `{python} CallPrice.ratio_str` prompt tokens. This severe hardware asymmetry explains why output token volume governs latency in single-agent execution (principle \ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding})\index{Principle!output-bound latency}. Keep in mind that this ratio reflects weight-dominated, unbatched decode against peak-throughput prefill rather than a measured cloud service rate or commercial billing tier; @sec-vol3-appendix-inference-roofline derives both floors in detail and formalizes their operating boundaries.

This analytical budget charges each prompt token once at the prefill floor and reserves one decode floor step for each generated token. We treat this as an idealized hardware baseline rather than a substitute for wall-clock measurement: it omits network transit, queueing delay, attention quadratics, and runtime software overhead. It also assumes standard autoregressive generation without speculative decoding. In production, a serving system that batches concurrent client requests, distributes model weights across tensor-parallel accelerators, or reuses cached attention state substantially alters the relationship between token count and elapsed time. The analytical estimate is therefore ideal for comparing interface formats and output volumes, but certifying a production deadline requires measuring latency directly under realistic serving load.

Applying this baseline to the first repair turn demonstrates the structural dominance of output tokens. A prompt of `{python} CallPrice.s0_str` tokens contributes `{python} CallPrice.call1_pre_str` of prefill work, while generating a reply of `{python} CallPrice.k_turn_str` tokens contributes `{python} CallPrice.call1_dec_str` of decode execution. The total call estimate is `{python} CallPrice.call1_total_str`. Although output constitutes only `{python} CallPrice.call1_tok_pct_str` of the call's total tokens, it accounts for `{python} CallPrice.call1_out_pct_str` of the required processing time. Pruning redundant output tokens therefore reduces overall latency far more effectively than removing an identical number of prompt tokens. At the same time, an agent benefits from a cheaper invocation only if the model still receives sufficient diagnostic context to generate a correct candidate; engineers must prune verbosity from the output format, not critical evidence from the prompt.

### Multi-turn trajectory cost accumulation {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-trajectory-cost-accumulation}

Even when individual turns produce concise outputs, a multi-turn trajectory can still generate an immense prompt ingestion workload. Consider an agent runtime that maintains an append-only execution log and re-transmits the full cumulative history on every invocation. If the initial turn contains $S_{\text{base}}$ prompt tokens and each subsequent turn appends $\Delta$ tokens of combined model output and tool observations, a trajectory spanning a horizon of $H$ turns submits:

$$S_{\text{sent}} = \sum_{j=0}^{H-1} \left(S_{\text{base}} + j\Delta\right) = H S_{\text{base}} + \Delta \frac{H(H-1)}{2}$$ {#eq-vol3-trajectory-resend}

prompt tokens in total. The quadratic growth in @eq-vol3-trajectory-resend arises directly from the naive strategy of repeatedly re-sending accumulated history, rather than from an intrinsic requirement of agentic reasoning. Implementing sliding-window context buffers, trimming redundant tool payloads, or summarizing historical turns transforms this workload. Furthermore, a stateful serving interface can maintain conversation state on the server, avoiding redundant network re-transmission even when the model's active attention window spans the full trajectory.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/resend_vs_prefix_reuse_margin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two curves of cumulative input tokens from turn 1 to turn 30. A red curve labeled re-sent bends upward to 892.5k. A green line labeled fresh prefill rises slowly to 51.5k."}

*Re-sent input grows with the square of the horizon; prefix reuse keeps fresh prefill linear.*
:::

Fortunately, repeated prompt input does not necessitate repeated matrix computation. **Prefix caching**\index{Prefix cache!economics} enables the inference engine to retain and reuse previously computed Key-Value (KV) activations for prompt prefixes that remain identical across consecutive requests [@zheng2024sglang]. Successful KV reuse requires an exact match across token IDs, model weights, sampling parameters, and positional encodings, as well as sufficient GPU memory to retain the cache blocks. Modifying an early system prompt instruction or altering a tool schema invalidates all downstream cached activations from that modification point onward. Even identical source text fails to hit the cache if tokenizer configurations, chat templates, or special tokens diverge.

To quantify the benefits of prefix reuse, assume an inference service that caches all preceding prompt prefixes but runs fresh prefill over each newly appended turn suffix. This newly appended suffix contains the model's previous response and the subsequent tool output. Across all $H$ turns, the cumulative number of prompt tokens requiring fresh prefill drops to $S_{\text{base}}+(H-1)\Delta$. This baseline conservatively assumes the runtime does not preserve the KV activations generated during decoding; advanced engines can retain those generated activations as well, avoiding fresh prefill over earlier model outputs. Holding these assumptions constant isolates the exact architectural benefit of prefix caching.

::: {#nbk-02-price-of-a-trajectory .callout-notebook title="The price of an append-only trajectory"}

**Problem**: A coding agent runs `{python} CallPrice.turns_str` turns. Its first prompt has `{python} CallPrice.s0_str` tokens, each turn appends `{python} CallPrice.delta_str` tokens, and each call emits `{python} CallPrice.k_turn_str` output tokens. Assume that every prompt fits the service's context limit and that compatible earlier prompt state remains available for reuse. How much input does the trajectory supply, and how does prompt-prefix reuse change its estimated processing work?

**Math**: Applying the arithmetic series in @eq-vol3-trajectory-resend gives `{python} CallPrice.resend_math` prompt tokens. Total output is `{python} CallPrice.output_math` tokens. Without reuse, input therefore accounts for `{python} CallPrice.input_share_str` of the combined input and output token count, although it does not account for that share of processing time.

With prompt-prefix reuse, fresh prefill covers `{python} CallPrice.cached_math` tokens. Dividing the original input count by this fresh-prefill count gives a `{python} CallPrice.cache_saving_mult_str` reduction. At the reference input allowance, the prefill-work estimate falls from `{python} CallPrice.pre_nocache_str` to `{python} CallPrice.pre_cache_str`. The output allowance remains `{python} CallPrice.dec_total_str`; caching earlier input does not remove the task's new responses.

**Systems insight**: Append-only context makes input work grow with the square of the horizon. Doubling the trajectory to `{python} CallPrice.turns_2x_str` turns multiplies re-sent input by `{python} CallPrice.growth_nocache_mult_str` but fresh prefill under prefix reuse by only `{python} CallPrice.growth_cache_mult_str`, because reuse converts quadratic growth into a linear trajectory. Prefix reuse therefore serves as the primary lever for minimizing the input component of $C_{\text{attempt}}$ in the cost per accepted task (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task), with its value compounding as horizons lengthen. While caching preserves the full decision context without loss of information, cache eviction and cross-worker request routing can dilute these theoretical savings in production.

:::

The two metrics in this calculation address different dimensions of system performance. Wall-clock latency governs the end-to-end responsiveness experienced by a single agent trajectory. Because each sequential turn depends strictly on the outcome of prior tool executions, an agent cannot parallelize its own dependent turns; every output token remains a sequential step on the critical execution path, even when the server concurrently batches that step with other requests. Computational work, by contrast, dictates cluster throughput, hardware provisioning, and aggregate operational expenditure. When a serving cluster batches dozens of concurrent streams, the memory weight reads are amortized across requests. Under high batching, the amortized service time per decoded token drops from the memory-bandwidth floor toward the compute-bound arithmetic limit $2P/R_{\text{peak}}$ of @eq-vol3-fm-token-floors—approaching the exact same efficiency as prompt prefill (@sec-vol3-appendix-inference-roofline). In this regime, total cluster workload scales directly with aggregate token volume. For an append-only agent, that token volume is overwhelmingly dominated by re-sent prompt history. Consequently, completion output length dictates individual agent turn latency, whereas uncached prompt prefill dictates aggregate serving work, assuming the cluster maintains high batching and provides adequate memory capacity for attention state.

This structural trade-off directly characterizes the automated repair agent, whose downstream consumer is a compilation and test pipeline that must wait for a syntactically complete response. In contrast, the customer support agent (\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}) streams output tokens to an interactive user. Running the exact same model on identical hardware exposes entirely different latency bottlenecks across these two operational archetypes.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-fm-latency-by-archetype
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BINDING LATENCY TERM: SUPPORT TURN VS. REPAIR CALL (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: lhs-02-call-latency-by-archetype, @eq-vol3-call-latency.
# │ Goal: Show that the support agent binds on TTFT and the repair agent on
# │       output length under the same reference floors.
# │ Show: Support prefill and reply time, streaming token rate, fresh prefill
# │       with a shared policy prefix; repair first-turn output share.
# │ How: Reuse CallPrice's per-token floors (registry model and accelerator);
# │      support-turn lengths come from the Agents.Support.CustomerOps
# │      workload profile (teaching assumptions, not measurements).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_count, fmt_time

class LatencyByArchetype:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_pre = CallPrice.t_pre  # registry-derived prefill floor per prompt token
    t_dec = CallPrice.t_dec  # registry-derived decode floor per output token
    support = Agents.Support.CustomerOps
    sup_prompt = support.session_context.to("token").magnitude  # policy, customer record, conversation
    sup_shared = support.shared_prefix.to("token").magnitude  # prefix identical across sessions
    sup_reply = support.reply_tokens.to("token").magnitude  # support reply tokens

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    sup_prefill = (sup_prompt * t_pre).to(second)
    sup_reply_t = (sup_reply * t_dec).to(second)
    stream_rate = (1 / t_dec).to(1 / second).magnitude  # tokens per second
    sup_fresh = sup_prompt - sup_shared
    sup_prefill_cached = (sup_fresh * t_pre).to(second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(sup_prefill < 1 * second < sup_reply_t, "Prefill well under a second; full reply takes seconds")
    check(sup_prefill_cached < sup_prefill / 3, "Shared-prefix reuse removes most support prefill")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    sup_prompt_str = fmt_count(sup_prompt)
    sup_shared_str = fmt_count(sup_shared)
    sup_fresh_str = fmt_count(sup_fresh)
    sup_reply_str = fmt_count(sup_reply)
    sup_prefill_str = fmt_time(sup_prefill, unit=second, precision=2)
    sup_reply_t_str = fmt_time(sup_reply_t, unit=second, precision=1)
    stream_rate_str = fmt_count(round(stream_rate))
    sup_prefill_cached_str = fmt_time(sup_prefill_cached, unit=second, precision=2)
```

::: {#lhs-02-call-latency-by-archetype .callout-lighthouse title="Call latency for two lighthouses"}

**Support agent**: A customer-operations turn submits an `{python} LatencyByArchetype.sup_prompt_str`-token prompt (consisting of policy documentation, customer account history, and recent dialogue) and streams an `{python} LatencyByArchetype.sup_reply_str`-token response to a human user in a live chat interface. Based on our reference hardware floors, prefill takes `{python} LatencyByArchetype.sup_prefill_str` and generating the full reply requires `{python} LatencyByArchetype.sup_reply_t_str`. However, token streaming displays the initial words immediately following queueing and prefill; the remaining tokens arrive at approximately `{python} LatencyByArchetype.stream_rate_str` tokens per second, which easily outpaces human reading speed. The binding constraint for user experience is therefore TTFT. When `{python} LatencyByArchetype.sup_shared_str` prompt tokens represent a common prefix of system instructions, organizational policies, and tool definitions shared across all concurrent sessions, prefix caching leaves only `{python} LatencyByArchetype.sup_fresh_str` tokens of fresh prefill—requiring just `{python} LatencyByArchetype.sup_prefill_cached_str`. In a loaded cluster, admission queueing rapidly becomes the dominant contributor to first-token latency.

**Repair agent**: The initial repair turn commits `{python} CallPrice.call1_out_pct_str` of its estimated hardware work to generating a `{python} CallPrice.k_turn_str`-token response. The agent runtime can parse, validate, and execute the generated patch only after receiving the entire payload. The binding constraint is decode duration, and the primary optimization lever is the compactness of the requested code representation.

**Systems insight**: Systems engineers must optimize the specific latency term that binds each workload: TTFT (queueing plus uncached prefill) for the interactive support agent, and total decode duration (output token volume) for the automated repair agent. Misdirecting optimization efforts targets metrics that neither user nor runtime waits on: truncating a customer support reply barely accelerates the appearance of the first word, while caching the prompt of an automated repair agent barely shortens the multi-second wait for a full patch to compile.

:::

Retaining intermediate activations in memory introduces an explicit storage cost. Caching a long prefix occupies GPU high-bandwidth memory that cannot be allocated to concurrent request batches. Holding that KV state active across long external tool invocations pins valuable memory while the GPU sits idle. When memory pressure triggers cache eviction, the serving system discards intermediate attention activations rather than the underlying context; the agent runtime can always reconstruct the prompt from its local logs, albeit at the cost of recomputing the prefill forward pass. Context selection and KV-cache management thus represent two distinct system decisions: context engineering determines what evidence the model observes, whereas cache retention policies govern whether storing derived attention state is worth the memory footprint.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Context selection and prefix layout are developed in @sec-vol3-context-engineering; capacity and retention policies for reusable attention state belong to @sec-vol3-kv-cache.
:::

Wall-clock latency, hardware compute work, and billed API cost represent distinct accounting dimensions. Commercial inference providers typically bill uncached prompt tokens, cached prompt tokens, and generated completion tokens at widely divergent rates, whereas on-premise infrastructure amortizes fixed hardware acquisition and power costs across dynamic utilization. Consequently, token-count ratios do not directly mirror monetary expense. At the full task horizon, end-to-end expenditure also encompasses failed tool executions, retry attempts, sandboxed validation runs, and idle accelerator reservations during tool waits. The analytical per-call estimate provides only one fundamental building block of this comprehensive systems budget.

::: {#chk-02-price-of-a-call .callout-checkpoint title="Pricing calls and trajectories"}

A call's token count and its elapsed execution time quantify distinct facets of the overall system budget.

- [ ] **Measurement boundary**: If the time to first token already accounts for sampling and delivering the initial token, how many subsequent token-generation intervals remain in a completed completion of length $K$?
- [ ] **Horizon estimate**: If an agent trajectory triples to `{python} CallPrice.turns_3x_str` turns under fixed $S_{\text{base}}$ and $\Delta$, estimate the growth factor for uncached re-sent input vs. fresh prefill under prefix caching. Which term dictates whether scaling to longer trajectories remains computationally viable?
- [ ] **Reuse assumptions**: How does the analytical work estimate change if the inference server evicts the cached prefix from GPU memory during a blocking tool execution?
- [ ] **Cost denominator**: Why does an overwhelming majority of input tokens fail to produce an equivalent majority of financial cost when providers bill cached input and generated output at starkly different rates?
- [ ] **Interface estimate**: A full-file replacement requires `{python} CallPrice.k_full_str` output tokens, whereas a localized diff requires only `{python} CallPrice.k_diff_str`. At our reference decode floor, which interface alternative can realistically operate within a `{python} CallPrice.deadline_str` latency deadline? Why is this analytical roofline model insufficient on its own to guarantee real-world SLA compliance?

:::

Deconstructing the model invocation budget exposes two primary sources of computational waste: generating superfluous tokens that the downstream interface does not require, and recomputing prompt representations that the serving system could readily cache. Yet optimizing these efficiency levers does not guarantee task success; a compact diff that fails to compile or a cached prompt that leads to an incorrect edit wastes the entire invocation. Selecting an optimal agent interface demands evaluating candidate patch quality, downstream failure modes, and end-to-end resource consumption under identical operational benchmarks.
## Interface Benchmarking {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-interface-design}

When an automated repair agent modifies connection-pool locking logic, its output payload does not need to repeat the entire source file. The model could emit a fully rewritten file, or it could target a specific code block and emit only the replacement text. Emitting a localized edit consumes far fewer generation tokens by omitting unchanged code, but it creates an operational dependency: the execution runtime must locate the exact target coordinates in the target file. Choosing an interface is therefore not a superficial formatting choice; it directly determines both the computational cost of generating a candidate and the operational preconditions required for the runtime to apply it.

High schema parse rates alone cannot validate an interface design. A whole-file replacement might parse into valid JSON yet arrive long after the service deadline because the model spent tens of seconds generating unchanged lines. Conversely, a compact diff might arrive in milliseconds yet fail to match its target anchors against current repository state. Neither outcome delivers an accepted repair. A rigorous empirical comparison must track the model call's completion status, account for all compute resources consumed across retries, and validate the resulting artifact against uniform acceptance criteria.

### Interface design dimensions {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-interface-design-dimensions}

Representation granularity dictates how much context the model must emit to describe a mutation. At one extreme, a whole-file representation returns the entire file content, re-emitting hundreds of lines of untouched code alongside the modification. At the other extreme, a localized edit supplies only a target locator and the delta relative to the baseline file. Consider an anchored search-and-replace edit: it specifies an exact snippet of source text to find and the replacement text to substitute. If that anchor string is missing from the file or matches multiple locations, the runtime cannot infer a unique mutation. Rewriting the entire file eliminates anchor-matching ambiguities, but it introduces a different validation burden: the runtime must ensure the model did not silently overwrite unrelated functions or drop concurrent modifications made by other processes.

Serialization represents a distinct and orthogonal design dimension. Either granularity can use JSON: one object might store a target path and complete source buffer, while another stores a path, a search block, and a replacement snippet. Custom delimiters, such as Markdown code fences or unified diff headers, can frame either payload just as easily. The actual token overhead depends on tokenizer vocabulary and structural markers, not on common folklore that JSON is inherently bloated while patch syntax is always compact. Emitting thousands of tokens for an unmodified file is a penalty imposed by coarse representation granularity, not by the serialization format wrapping it.

The constraint mechanism introduces a third independent axis. An agent architecture can elicit structured outputs through fine-tuning, in-context demonstrations, or runtime grammar masking during token decoding. These mechanisms can also operate together; for example, fine-tuned models frequently run under grammar masks to prevent syntax drift. The formal language guarantees established in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-grammar-constrained ensure that generated tokens conform to a specified grammar, but they guarantee grammatical form, not execution semantics. A grammar mask cannot guarantee that an anchor snippet exists within the repository, nor that the proposed patch repairs the underlying race condition. If an evaluation alters both serialization framing and constraint methods simultaneously, it benchmarks bundled interface variants rather than isolating the causal impact of any single architectural choice.

### Matched-budget comparison {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-matched-budget-comparison}

To evaluate competing interfaces fairly, an experimental harness must enforce matched budgets across all trials. In our connection-pool repair benchmark, every trial starts from an identical repository snapshot and defect description. We hold constant the model weights, sampling parameters, diagnostic tooling, and acceptance test suites. Crucially, each interface operates under identical resource ceilings (such as maximum wall-clock time and token allocations) and the same retry policy. Instruction prompts and response payloads will naturally exhibit different token counts, because prompt overhead and verbosity are intrinsic properties of the interface under test. Matched budgets do not require equal token consumption across designs; rather, they subject each candidate to identical operating boundaries and accounting rules.

The accounting boundary must be defined explicitly. An invocation deadline measures single-turn inference latency, concluding when the runtime receives and normalizes the model's generated response. A task deadline governs the complete agent lifecycle, including payload parsing, workspace patching, test compilation, and test execution. Every retry, unparsable output, and failing test execution draws against this cumulative task budget. Benchmarks that grant free retries following malformed responses subsidize brittle interfaces and corrupt comparative latency metrics.

To pinpoint system failures without masking catastrophic errors, the benchmark harness must decouple intermediate execution stages from final task acceptance (@tbl-vol3-interface-evaluation). The total number of initiated trials must remain the denominator for all top-level success metrics. Discarding unparsable responses or timed-out calls artificially inflates reported accuracy. Conditional rates—such as the proportion of cleanly applied edits that pass functional tests—serve as valuable diagnostic telemetry, but engineers must always state the conditioning filter explicitly.

| Measurement         | What the trial records                                                                       | What it does not establish                                 |
|:--------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------|
| Invocation outcome  | Completion status, elapsed time, and token usage                                             | That a delivered candidate is valid                        |
| Structural validity | Whether a completed payload parses and satisfies the required schema                         | That its values describe the current environment           |
| Applicability       | Whether the authorized edit identifies its target and can be applied to the expected version | That the resulting program repairs the defect              |
| Acceptance evidence | Results of the same required checks on the resulting artifact                                | Correctness beyond the checks' coverage                    |
| Resource use        | All calls and checks charged to the trial, including failed attempts                         | A benefit unless accepted outcomes justify the expenditure |
: **Interface evaluation measurements**: Distinct observations prevent a formatting improvement from being mistaken for a task-level improvement. The same task fixtures, acceptance standard, and resource ceilings govern each design. {#tbl-vol3-interface-evaluation tbl-colwidths="[23,39,38]"}

Production serving conditions must also be recorded alongside payload statistics. Shared inference infrastructure introduces substantial latency variance: KV-cache hits, dynamic batching contention, and host-level queueing delays alter observed wall-clock execution even when prompt and completion lengths remain constant. A few favorable measurements during quiet periods do not prove deadline reliability. In shared production clusters, tail latency governs service-level objective violations, because the slowest requests dictate pipeline throughput [@dean2013tail]. The immediate engineering question is whether an interface representation leaves sufficient headroom under the tail-latency envelope to generate and validate candidate fixes. We examine formal experimental methodology and uncertainty estimation in @sec-vol3-evaluation.

### A deadline-constrained representation choice {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-deadline-representation-choice}

Applying the per-token cost model highlights the severe latency penalty of emitting unchanged text, tracing performance bottlenecks directly to interface granularity rather than serialization envelopes.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/representation_deadline_margin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal bars against a dashed red 15 s deadline line with a pale red zone beyond it. Whole file: a thin light-blue prompt segment and a long dark-blue output segment totaling 39.6 s. Local edit: short segments totaling 2.3 s. A legend marks prompt and output."}

*Generating unchanged code, not reading the prompt, pushes the whole file past the deadline.*
:::

::: {#nbk-02-quantitative-interface-evaluation-under-an .callout-notebook title="A repair representation under an invocation deadline"}

**Problem**: A repair invocation begins with `{python} CallPrice.s0_str` baseline context tokens and operates under an invocation deadline of `{python} CallPrice.deadline_str`.
